title: Do contractionary monetary policy shocks expand shadow banking?
authors: Benjamin Nelson; Gabor Pinter; Konstantinos Theodoridis
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Dealers and market makers; Private credit and private equity; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: Using VAR models on US data from 1966–2007, the authors find that contractionary monetary policy shocks persistently reduce commercial bank asset growth but increase shadow bank asset growth and securitisation activity, a 'waterbed effect' they explain with a New Keynesian model featuring both banking sectors. The findings suggest monetary policy cannot uniformly curtail financial sector leverage and that regulatory tools specifically targeting shadow banking are needed alongside monetary policy.

title: Interactions among high-frequency traders
authors: Evangelos Benos; James Brugler; Erik Hjalmarsson; Filip Zikes
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Market dysfunction; Interconnectedness and concentration; Equity markets
summary: Using transaction-level data on individual high-frequency trading firms in the UK equity market, the authors find that HFT order flows exhibit significantly higher commonality than investment bank order flows, but this commonality is associated with permanent price impacts suggesting it is information-based rather than causing price dislocations. The paper concludes that correlated HFT trading activity reflects informed trading that improves price efficiency rather than creating excess volatility or market dysfunction.

title: On a tight leash: does bank organisational structure matter for macroprudential spillovers?
authors: Piotr Danisewicz; Dennis Reinhardt; Rhiannon Sowerbutts
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Margin and collateral calls; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: This paper examines how the organizational structure of foreign bank affiliates affects cross-border spillovers of macroprudential regulation. The authors find that branches of multinational banks reduce interbank lending growth by 6.3 percentage points more than subsidiaries following home-country capital requirement tightening, but this effect is short-lived and does not extend to non-bank lending or other regulatory types.

title: Filtered historical simulation Value-at-Risk models and their competitors
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Value-at-Risk models
summary: The paper examines filtered historical simulation (FHS) Value-at-Risk models used to estimate risk in financial portfolios and set margin requirements. It analyzes how FHS models incorporate recent market conditions to produce conditional risk estimates, discusses their procyclicality, and considers implications for initial margin requirements on derivatives.

title: Innovations in the Bank's provision of liquidity insurance via Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) operations
authors: Tarkus Frost; Nick Govier; Tom Horn
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Repo markets
summary: The Bank of England has redesigned its Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) facility to provide automatic and flexible liquidity insurance by incorporating lessons from auction theory. The ILTR mechanism now automatically adjusts both the quantity of liquidity supplied and its allocation across collateral types in response to stress, offering longer maturities and cheaper rates against a wider range of eligible collateral.

title: Did Quantitative Easing boost bank lending?
authors: Nick Butt; Rohan Churm; Michael McMahon
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The authors test whether UK quantitative easing boosted bank lending through a bank lending channel but find no statistically significant effect. They attribute this to high churn in deposits created by QE, which prevented banks from viewing deposits as stable funding; instead, QE operated through portfolio rebalancing, with non-banks using deposits to purchase higher-yielding assets.

title: What do we know about non-bank interconnectedness?
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Interconnectedness and concentration; Repo markets; Bank–non-bank linkages
summary: Using granular regulatory data on bank exposures to non-banks, the authors find that banks' direct credit exposures to non-bank financial institutions are small relative to bank capital, but some non-banks have entered the core of the repo network. Hedge funds are not conducting significant leveraged credit intermediation, but asset managers, insurers and pension funds are obtaining leverage through repo borrowing against government bonds.

title: Has corporate bond market liquidity fallen?
authors: Yuliya Baranova; Louisa Chen; Nicholas Vause
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Market liquidity; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: Using a structural VAR model comparing pre-crisis and post-crisis periods, the authors find that dealer inventories now respond less to asset manager demand shocks for high-yield corporate bonds, while spreads and subsequent issuance declines respond more, suggesting reduced market-making capacity. The findings indicate that corporate bond market liquidity has deteriorated post-crisis, with dealers acting less as shock absorbers and prices adjusting more sharply to demand changes.

title: The special relationship: UK and US bond yields
central_concepts: Gilt market; US Treasury market
summary: UK and US government bond yields move highly together across maturities and time horizons, driven by correlated policy-rate expectations, global term premia, and spillovers from unconventional monetary policy. This co-movement matters because changes in US yields feed through to UK financing costs for households, firms and government, creating important international financial linkages for policymakers.

title: A heterogeneous agent model for assessing the effects of capital regulation on the interbank money market under a corridor system
central_concepts: Money markets; Corridor system; Capital regulation
summary: This paper develops a heterogeneous agent model to examine how prudential capital regulations affect overnight interbank money market interest rates under a corridor system. The results suggest that risk-weighted capital requirements tend to increase overnight rates while minimum leverage ratios tend to decrease them, with implications for central bank operational frameworks.

title: Over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, central clearing and financial stability
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Central counterparties; Interconnectedness and concentration; Margin and collateral calls
summary: OTC derivatives markets are systemically important and have grown significantly, with the UK as the dominant global centre. Central clearing through CCPs mitigates counterparty risk but concentrates it within CCPs, requiring strengthened prudential standards, stress testing, and international regulatory cooperation.

title: A sectoral framework for analysing money, credit and unconventional monetary policy
authors: James Cloyne; Ryland Thomas; Alex Tuckett; Samuel Wills
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Market-based finance; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The paper develops an empirical sectoral framework to analyse money and credit transmission mechanisms across households, corporates, and financial sectors, using the banking balance sheet as an organising principle. The framework is illustrated by examining how quantitative easing and credit market disturbances transmit through sectors to affect real activity and asset prices.

title: Rational and Behavioural Drivers of Financial Markets: the case of ‘search for yield’
central_concepts: Reaching for yield; Asset price volatility; Corporate bond markets; Financial stability risk
summary: The paper examines how 'search for yield'—investors taking on higher credit, liquidity, or duration risk to boost returns in a low-interest-rate environment—reflects a mix of rational economic responses and behavioural biases. It argues that while some risk-taking reflects fundamental monetary policy transmission and regulatory constraints, herd behaviour, myopia, and heuristics can amplify mispricing, potentially creating financial stability risks.

title: High-frequency trading and market quality: What’s the deal?
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity; Asset price volatility; Order anticipation
summary: High-frequency trading has evolved to account for 20-50% of volume in equities and has generally improved market quality by enhancing price efficiency and reducing bid-ask spreads. However, concerns remain about order anticipation strategies and whether the social benefits of HFT justify the substantial technology investments required.

title: Regulatory arbitrage in action: evidence from cross-border lending and macroprudential policy
central_concepts: Bank–non-bank linkages; Margin policy reforms; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: The paper finds evidence that macroprudential capital requirements are circumvented through cross-border borrowing from foreign banks, while lending standards are not similarly avoided. This regulatory arbitrage is stronger in banking systems where foreign affiliates operate as branches rather than subsidiaries, highlighting the need for stronger reciprocity frameworks in macroprudential policy.

title: Centralized trading, transparency and interest rate swap market liquidity: evidence from the implementation of the Dodd-Frank Act
authors: Evangelos Benos; Richard Payne; Michalis Vasios
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity; Data and transparency on non-banks
summary: The paper analyzes how the Dodd-Frank Act's mandate requiring US persons to trade interest rate swaps on centralized Swap Execution Facilities (SEFs) affected market liquidity and trading patterns. The authors find that SEF trading significantly improved liquidity and reduced execution costs for USD mandated contracts, but uneven global application of the regulation caused geographic fragmentation in EUR swap markets.

title: What explains the fall in sterling corporate bond issuance?
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Market liquidity; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: Sterling's share of global corporate bond issuance has collapsed from 6% in 2006 to under 2% in 2015, driven by structural changes including concentration of the sterling investor base, UK annuities reform reducing demand for long-dated debt, and competition from a developing euro corporate bond market. These trends threaten to create a downward spiral where lower issuance reduces liquidity, raising borrowing costs and further discouraging issuance, with particular adverse effects on smaller and lower-rated UK companies.

title: Monetary policy and volatility in the sterling money market
central_concepts: Money markets; Market liquidity; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The paper evaluates how reforms to the Bank of England's operating framework over 1997–2014 affected money market volatility, finding that the 2006 reserves averaging framework and 2009 floor system reduced overnight rate volatility. Despite these improvements, overnight volatility had minimal transmission to term rates critical for monetary policy transmission, suggesting that prioritising overnight volatility reduction may have limited macroeconomic benefits.

title: An agent-based model of dynamics in corporate bond trading
authors: Karen Braun-Munzinger; Zijun Liu; Arthur Turrell
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Dealers and market makers; Open-ended funds; Asset price volatility
summary: An agent-based model of the US corporate bond market shows that market maker sensitivity to demand shocks, momentum trading, and the growth of passive funds significantly influence yield overshooting and market procyclicality. The model demonstrates that redemption management tools can dampen shock propagation, while passive investment growth increases tail risk of large yield dislocations.

title: A comparative analysis of tools to limit the procyclicality of initial margin requirements
authors: David Murphy; Michalis Vasios; Nicholas Vause
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Procyclical margin; Derivatives markets
summary: The paper analyses tools to mitigate procyclical initial margin requirements on derivatives transactions, which burden market participants most severely in stressed conditions. Through simulation, the authors compare five tools and find that all reduce procyclicality to some extent, with optimal calibration depending on the trade-off between minimizing procyclicality and avoiding overmargining in low-volatility periods.

title: Liquidity determinants in the UK gilt market
central_concepts: Gilt market; Market liquidity; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: Using proprietary transactional data from primary dealers, the authors show that gilt market liquidity is significantly determined by dealer balance sheet constraints, funding costs, and inter-dealer market frictions. They document that reduced inter-dealer trading and increased dealer concentration substantially raise execution costs for non-dealers, with economically significant daily impacts of £700K–£1.5 million and £270K–£1 million respectively at peak crisis periods.

title: Have reforms to the BOE’s operating framework reduced money market volatility, and does this matter for monetary policy transmission?
central_concepts: Money markets; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The Bank of England's reforms to its operating framework have reduced overnight money market volatility by around 90% since the early 2000s, but the author finds little evidence that this volatility reduction affects term rates, which are more important for monetary policy transmission. The analysis suggests central banks might prioritize flexibility to accommodate changing liquidity conditions over reducing money market volatility.

title: The role of collateral in supporting liquidity
authors: Yuliya Baranova; Zijun Liu; Joseph Noss
central_concepts: Collateral and safe assets; Market liquidity; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Procyclicality
summary: The paper estimates how collateral supply and demand become imbalanced during market stress, and identifies two key risks: demand exceeding supply (crystallising at VIX ~44%) with moderate impact, and a more severe risk that dealer intermediation capacity falls short of that required to move collateral from suppliers to users. The analysis suggests that dealer constraints pose a greater threat to financial stability than simple supply-demand imbalance.

title: Forming strong bonds: dynamics in corporate bond markets
authors: Karen Braun-Munzinger; Zijun Liu; Arthur Turrell
central_concepts: Open-ended funds; Corporate bond markets; Liquidity mismatch; Fire sales; Run risk
summary: Using agent-based modelling of corporate bond markets, the authors show that shocks to expected credit loss rates trigger feedback loops where investor redemptions force fire sales that depress prices further, destroying wealth for remaining investors. They find that spreading redemptions over longer periods can significantly dampen these destabilising feedback loops, especially when investor flows are sensitive to fund performance.

title: When asset managers go MAD
central_concepts: Open-ended funds; Fire sales; Asset price volatility; Benchmarking and relative performance
summary: The paper uses game theory, specifically the prisoner's dilemma framework, to model how asset managers may face incentives to sell assets during financial stress even though coordinated holding would produce better collective outcomes. Benchmarking practices that tie manager reputation to relative performance amplify these incentives, creating a potential mechanism for fire sales and financial instability.

title: Collateral and market stress: what are the risks?
authors: Yuliya Baranova; Zijun Liu; Joseph Noss
central_concepts: Collateral and safe assets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Repo markets
summary: The paper identifies two risks from collateral dynamics in financial stress: demand temporarily exceeding supply (limited impact after price adjustment) and dealer balance-sheet constraints preventing collateral redistribution (severe impact on market functioning). The authors estimate that collateral shortage crystallises at VIX 44% and dealer intermediation capacity constraints at VIX 46%, with the latter posing greater financial stability risk due to its persistence.

title: Dis-integrating credit markets: diversification, securitization, and lending in a recovery
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Dealers and market makers; Credit to the real economy
summary: Using hurricane exposure as exogenous variation, the paper shows that local banks originate more mortgages and small business loans in affected areas during recovery, but sell a higher share of these mortgages into the secondary market compared to diversified banks. This reveals a pattern of specialization where loan origination stays with local banks exploiting local knowledge, while financing and risk transfer move to better-diversified secondary market participants.

title: Bitesize: 250 years of the bond-equity correlation
central_concepts: Bond-equity correlation; Gilt market; Collateral and safe assets
summary: Bond and equity returns have shifted from positive to negative correlation since the mid-2000s, reflecting reduced inflation concerns, increased demand for safe assets, and changes in monetary policy tools. This structural change means bonds now act as a hedge rather than a risky asset, a reversal of the 18th-20th century pattern.

title: Does market liquidity risk affect Euro corporate bond returns more seriously in stress periods?
authors: Wolfgang Aussenegg; Louisa Chen; Ranko Jelic; Dietmar Maringer
central_concepts: Market liquidity; Corporate bond markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: Using a regime-switching model on Euro corporate bonds from 2000-2014, the authors find that market liquidity risk reduces bond returns five times more strongly in stress regimes than normal regimes, and that dealers' funding constraints amplify this effect by reducing their market-making activity.

title: Unto us a lender of last resort is born: Overend Gurney goes bust in 1866
central_concepts: Money market funds; Liquidity mismatch; Run risk; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: The 1866 collapse of Overend Gurney, a bill broker operating like a money market fund, sparked a financial panic that threatened the entire system. The Bank of England's provision of liquidity against good collateral at a penalty rate, enabled by Chancellor indemnity to issue unbacked currency, arrested the panic and established the foundational principles of the lender-of-last-resort function.

title: A discrete choice model for large heterogeneous panels with interactive fixed effects with an application to the determinants of corporate bond issuance
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Credit to the real economy; Asset price volatility
summary: The paper develops a discrete choice model for large heterogeneous panels to estimate the effect of funding costs on corporate bond issuance by US firms between 1990 and 2015. The authors find that yields are negatively related to bond issuance for non-financial firms, with a larger effect in the pre-crisis period, particularly for low-rated firms.

title: Market liquidity, closeout procedures and initial margin for CCPs
authors: Fernando Cerezetti; Anannit Sumawong; Ujwal Shreyas; Emmanouil Karimalis
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Market liquidity; Closeout procedures and default management; Margin and collateral calls; Funding constraints
summary: The paper develops a framework for evaluating how different closeout strategies expose central counterparties to varying levels of market risk and liquidation costs when clearing members default. Using ten years of OTC interest rate swap data, the authors derive an empirically efficient hedging strategy that minimizes total risk while accounting for real-world market constraints and transaction costs.

title: Capital Inflows: The Good, the Bad and the Bubbly
authors: Glenn Hoggarth; Carsten Jung; Dennis Reinhardt
central_concepts: Capital inflows; Debt flows and loan stability; Bank–non-bank linkages; Market-based finance
summary: The paper analyzes how different types of capital flows to emerging market economies respond to financial stress, finding that debt flows are more volatile than equity flows, foreign bank flows are more volatile than non-bank flows, and foreign-currency-denominated flows are more unstable than local-currency flows. The authors show that macroprudential policies, particularly higher bank capital ratios, can reduce the sensitivity of capital inflows to global volatility and enhance financial stability.

title: Bitesize: Tantrums, massacres and bond market reversals
central_concepts: Gilt market; US Treasury market; Asset price volatility
summary: UK gilt and US Treasury yields rose sharply in late 2016 following Brexit concerns and the US presidential election, with moves comparable in magnitude and pace to historical episodes like the 2013 taper tantrum and 1994 bond massacre. The authors suggest these reversals reflect fundamental patterns in bond market momentum and trading dynamics rather than being unprecedented events.

title: Low for long: what does this mean for defined-benefit pensions in the UK?
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Leverage; Procyclicality
summary: Low growth and persistently low interest rates increase defined-benefit pension liabilities more than assets, widening funding gaps and creating financial stability risks through pension funds' search for yield across alternative assets. While the direct solvency challenges to DB schemes do not immediately threaten stability, indirect risks could emerge from correlated search-for-yield behaviour by multiple financial institutions and shifts in household savings toward riskier assets.

title: Macroprudential policy beyond banking
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Open-ended funds; Leverage; Liquidity mismatch; Run risk; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: Since 2008, market-based financing in the EU has nearly doubled while bank balance sheets have stagnated, shifting systemic risks beyond the banking sector. The authors argue that macroprudential policy must extend beyond banks to address risks from leverage, liquidity mismatch, interconnectedness, and misaligned incentives across all financial intermediaries, particularly investment funds and securities financing markets.

title: Of Goosebumps and CCP default funds
authors: Fernando V. Cerezetti; Luis Antonio Barron G. Vicente
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Financial stability risk
summary: The paper examines whether default funds in central counterparties (CCPs) remain an effective risk management tool or are merely historical relics. It argues that while default funds have evolved from static to dynamic risk-adjusted models, they require continued refinement in replenishment procedures, coverage standards, and mutualisation schemes to address free-riding effects and capital cost problems.

title: Big Data jigsaws for Central Banks – the impact of the Swiss franc de-pegging
authors: Olga Cielinska; Andreas Joseph; Ujwal Shreyas; John Tanner; Michalis Vasios
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; FX and FX swap markets; Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity; Granular transaction data
summary: The authors use granular transaction-level data from over-the-counter derivatives markets to analyse the Swiss National Bank's unexpected de-pegging of the euro-Swiss franc in January 2015, reconstructing trading and exposure networks to understand intraday price movements, liquidity conditions, and market fragmentation. They find that poor dealer liquidity provision caused sharp price overshoots on the event day, and that inter-dealer activity declined significantly in the months following, leading to increased market fragmentation.

title: Bitesize: Blink and you’ve missed it: French government bond ‘mini flash’
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Market liquidity; Market dysfunction; Asset price volatility
summary: On 16 February 2017, French government bond futures experienced a 'mini flash' event with yields falling 11 basis points in 85 seconds during a period of illiquidity, before retracing within eight minutes, with no clear consensus on the cause. The event highlights vulnerabilities in traditionally deep and liquid markets, alongside similar episodes in sterling, US equities, and US Treasuries.

title: The impact of Solvency II regulations on life insurers’ investment behaviour
authors: Graeme Douglas; Joseph Noss; Nicholas Vause
central_concepts: Insurers; Macroprudential policy for non-banks; Margin and collateral calls; Procyclicality
summary: This paper develops a structural model of UK life insurers' asset allocation decisions to assess how Solvency II regulations affect their investment behaviour. It finds that Solvency II's risk margin design may encourage insurers to de-risk and sell long-term risky assets following falls in risk-free interest rates, potentially amplifying procyclical investment behaviour.

title: Dealer intermediation, market liquidity and the impact of regulatory reform
authors: Yuliya Baranova; Zijun Liu; Tamarah Shakir
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity; Margin policy reforms; Corporate bond markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: The paper develops a model of dealer intermediation in bond markets showing that post-crisis regulatory reforms, particularly leverage ratio requirements, increase liquidity premia by around 40 basis points in normal times but enhance dealer resilience in stress. Once the greater stability of market liquidity and dealer balance sheets is accounted for, the net benefit of regulation remains positive despite higher intermediation costs.

title: Pension fund deficit risk
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Asset price volatility; Deficit volatility
summary: UK defined-benefit pension funds have become large holders of bonds, increasing the correlation of their assets with their bond-like liabilities and reducing deficit volatility. This asset-liability matching behaviour dampens near-term deficit swings but could, if sustained at scale, pressure bond yields downward through further shifts toward bonds in pension fund portfolios.

title: Central counterparty auction design
central_concepts: Central counterparties
summary: This paper analyzes auction design mechanisms for managing clearing member defaults in central counterparties (CCPs), comparing sealed-bid auction formats and their implications for loss allocation and financial stability. The authors propose a second-price auction with loss-sharing design that balances revenue recovery with efficient portfolio assignment while reducing adverse externalities on surviving members.

title: Borderline: judging the adequacy of return distribution estimation techniques in initial margin models
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Derivatives markets; Volatility estimation
summary: The paper develops a new method for validating initial margin models used in derivatives markets by testing whether models accurately predict the worst loss over the margin period of risk, rather than relying solely on backtesting at fixed confidence intervals. The technique is applied to various volatility estimation methods and provides a more discriminating way to select acceptable model parameters than conventional approaches.

title: Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme: design, operation and impact
authors: Thomas Belsham; Alex Rattan; Rebecca Maher
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Market-based finance; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: The Bank of England's Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme, announced in August 2016, was designed to lower corporate borrowing costs and stimulate investment through purchases of up to £10 billion of sterling corporate bonds. The scheme appears to have successfully reduced corporate bond spreads by around 20 basis points, increased issuance, and improved market liquidity in the sterling corporate bond market.

title: Reducing counterparty credit risk in uncleared markets – but what are the costs?
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Margin and collateral calls; Collateral and safe assets
summary: Initial margin requirements for uncleared derivatives reduce counterparty credit risk but introduce new vulnerabilities including liquidity mismatches, operational risks in collateral custody and segregation, and concentration risks from reliance on unregulated service providers. The paper argues regulators must rethink risk frameworks as collateral replaces capital as the primary risk mitigant.

title: Eight centuries of the risk-free rate bond market reversals from the Venetians to the VaR shock
central_concepts: US Treasury market; Asset price volatility; Market liquidity; Monetary policy transmission via markets; Market dysfunction
summary: This paper constructs a 700-year dataset of global risk-free rates and identifies nine major bond bull markets, finding that the current bull market originating in 1981 is the third longest on record and reached historically low yields in July 2016. Analysis of three 20th-century bond market reversals shows that inflation-driven reversals inflict the longest losses, while central bank miscommunication and curve steepening dynamics also drive sharp market moves.

title: Investor behaviour and reaching for yield: evidence from the sterling corporate bond market
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Dealers and market makers; Insurers; Hedge funds; Open-ended funds; Reaching for yield; Procyclicality
summary: Using transaction-level data from the sterling corporate bond market, the authors find that insurance companies, hedge funds and asset managers typically buy bonds when yields rise, but asset managers reverse to selling during stress (the 2013 taper tantrum), while dealers act as countercyclical liquidity providers. The paper also documents 'reaching for yield' behaviour across investor types, with portfolios tilted towards higher-risk bonds, raising financial stability concerns about procyclical amplification.

title: Do investors amplify or cushion corporate bond market sell-offs?
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Open-ended funds; Dealers and market makers; Procyclicality
summary: The paper uses FCA transaction data to examine how different investor types in the sterling corporate bond market respond to yield changes. Asset managers, insurance companies, and hedge funds typically buy bonds when yields rise (countercyclical behaviour), but during the 2013 taper tantrum they switched to selling bonds (procyclical behaviour), potentially amplifying market stress and threatening credit supply to the real economy.

title: The leverage ratio and liquidity in the gilt and repo markets
central_concepts: Leverage; Gilt market; Repo markets; Market liquidity
summary: The paper investigates whether post-crisis leverage ratio regulations reduced liquidity in UK gilt and gilt repo markets. While market-level analysis shows gilt repo liquidity worsened during the period when leverage ratio policy was announced and gilt liquidity deteriorated conditional on funding costs and inventory risk, evidence of a direct causal link between the leverage ratio and reduced liquidity from dealer-level heterogeneity analysis is inconclusive.

title: Financial shocks, credit spreads and the international credit channel
central_concepts: Monetary policy transmission via markets; Credit to the real economy; Financial stability risk
summary: The paper provides empirical evidence that US financial shocks are transmitted internationally through an international credit channel, causing synchronized increases in credit spreads and economic slowdowns in countries like the UK. Unlike monetary policy shocks, financial shocks trigger sharper contractions in economic activity, demonstrating that credit market frictions and financial integration amplify cross-border spillovers.

title: Hedge funds and their prime brokers: developments since the financial crisis
central_concepts: Hedge funds; Dealers and market makers; Leverage
summary: Hedge funds have grown dramatically from $250 billion to $3.5 trillion in AUM since 2000, using leverage and prime brokerage financing to implement diverse strategies. The paper examines how hedge funds' interconnections with prime brokers, use of leverage, and potential for fire sales create financial stability risks, while noting post-crisis mitigations including business model adjustments and international regulatory reforms.

title: Unconventional monetary policy and the portfolio choice of international mutual funds
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Money market funds; Open-ended funds; Market maker of last resort; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: Unconventional monetary policy by major central banks causes international mutual fund managers to rebalance portfolios away from the country conducting UMP toward other developed markets, with little evidence of flows to emerging markets. Large-scale asset purchases have economically significant spillover effects on fund allocation, whereas announcement surprises have smaller effects, and fund managers play a negligible role in the risk-taking channel but contribute to portfolio balance transmission across developed markets.

title: Trimming the Hedge: How can CCPs efficiently manage a default?
authors: Fernando Cerezetti; Emmanouil Karimalis; Ujwal Shreyas; Anannit Sumawong
central_concepts: Central counterparties
summary: The paper investigates optimal hedging strategies for central counterparties (CCPs) managing the closeout of a defaulted member's portfolio, using EMIR trade repository data on sterling OTC interest rate swaps. The authors find that while more granular hedging reduces market risk exposure, transaction costs increase substantially, and the economically optimal strategy balances risk reduction against hedging costs rather than minimizing risk alone.

title: An elusive panacea? The impact of the regulatory valuation regime on insurers' investment behaviour
authors: Caterina Lepore; Misa Tanaka; David Humphry; Kallol Sen
central_concepts: Insurers; System-wide stress testing; Fair value accounting; Historical cost accounting; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: This paper examines how valuation regimes (historical cost, fair value, and hybrid) interact with solvency requirements to shape insurers' investment behaviour, finding that fair value and hybrid regimes can outperform historical cost only if regulators calibrate penalties based on supervisory information about asset quality. The analysis shows that historical cost encourages risk-shifting and gambling for resurrection, fair value can induce procyclical asset fire sales, and neither valuation adjustment alone solves both problems without appropriate regulatory responses.

title: Rethinking financial stability
authors: David Aikman; Andrew G Haldane; Marc Hinterschweiger; Sujit Kapadia
central_concepts: Financial stability risk; Market-based finance; Leverage; Liquidity mismatch; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: Post-crisis regulatory reforms have substantially increased bank capital and introduced macroprudential tools, but new evidence suggests the appropriate calibration of capital requirements remains ambiguous and a combination of regulatory metrics may be more effective than individual constraints in isolation. The authors highlight recurring policy questions including the balance between discretion and rules, the treatment of non-bank financial institutions (shadow banking), and the need for adaptive regulatory frameworks as the financial system evolves.

title: The 2016 Sterling Flash Episode
authors: Joseph Noss; Liam Crowley-Reidy; Lucas Pedace
central_concepts: FX and FX swap markets; Market liquidity; Market dysfunction; Asset price volatility
summary: The authors analyse the October 2016 sterling flash crash, a 10% currency depreciation in 40 seconds that was largely reversed within minutes. They find that the initial 1.8% movement is consistent with the observed order imbalance, but the larger subsequent price movement cannot be explained by trade-size effects alone, suggesting dealer liquidity withdrawal and futures-market dynamics also played a role.

title: Sterling money markets: beneath the surface
central_concepts: Money markets; Repo markets; Interest rate benchmarks
summary: The Bank of England's new Sterling Money Market data collection reveals that sterling money market activity is heavily concentrated in overnight transactions, with minimal activity in term deposits beyond one day. The analysis shows overnight unsecured deposits averaging £50 billion daily with stable rates, while longer-term deposits are scarce and volatile, supporting the transition from Libor to the SONIA overnight benchmark.

title: The impact of the Bank of England’s Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme on yield spreads
authors: Lena Boneva; Calebe de Roure; Ben Morley
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Yield spreads
summary: The Bank of England's August 2016 Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme reduced yield spreads of eligible sterling bonds by 13–14 basis points relative to foreign currency bonds issued by the same firms, and by 2–5 basis points relative to ineligible sterling bonds. The reduction operates through increased market liquidity and lower funding costs for eligible issuers.

title: What did the CBPS do to corporate bond yields?
authors: Calebe de Roure; Ben Morley; Lena Boneva
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Corporate bond markets
summary: The Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme (CBPS) announcement in August 2016 caused spreads on eligible sterling corporate bonds to tighten by approximately 13 basis points relative to comparable foreign-currency bonds of the same issuers, using a difference-in-differences methodology. This large announcement effect reflects the scheme's impact through portfolio rebalancing and reduced credit risk for participating corporates.

title: Algos all go?
authors: Francis Breedon; Louisa Chen; Angelo Ranaldo; Nicholas Vause
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity; Market dysfunction; FX and FX swap markets
summary: The authors analyse algorithmic trading's role in the January 2015 Swiss franc depegging using high-frequency FX market data, finding that algorithms provided less liquidity at worse prices and contributed near-zero price efficiency during the stress event. They conclude that market quality depends on diversity of trading strategies, and rising algorithmic trading may worsen outcomes in future shocks unless algorithm behaviour in stress improves.

title: Multiplex network analysis of the UK OTC derivatives market
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Margin and collateral calls; Central counterparties; Interconnectedness and concentration; Liquidity mismatch
summary: The paper analyses the UK OTC derivatives market using multiplex network analysis of interest rate, credit, and FX derivatives, developing centrality measures to assess institution vulnerability. A liquidity contagion model shows that in stress scenarios with small liquidity buffers, a small number of institutions can experience significant spillover effects from variation margin shocks.

title: The international transmission of monetary policy
authors: Claudia M Buch; Matthieu Bussiere; Linda Goldberg; Robert Hills
central_concepts: Bank–non-bank linkages; Monetary policy transmission via markets; Leverage
summary: This paper presents findings from a coordinated international study using confidential micro-banking data from 17 countries to examine how monetary policy shocks transmit across borders through bank lending. The research shows that international spillovers of monetary policy into bank lending are statistically pervasive but economically modest on average, though heterogeneity across banks can create large differences, with foreign currency funding and capitalization being key sources of variation in transmission.

title: Targeting financial stability: macroprudential or monetary policy?
central_concepts: Margin policy reforms; Financial stability risk; Procyclicality
summary: The paper develops a New Keynesian model to assess how macroprudential policy (the countercyclical capital buffer) and monetary policy interact to address financial stability risks from credit booms. It finds that the CCyB significantly improves outcomes compared to using interest rates alone, and that the two instruments typically act as substitutes in responding to credit booms, though a large market-based finance sector reduces the CCyB's effectiveness.

title: Central bank swap lines
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Bank–non-bank linkages; FX and FX swap markets; Liquidity mismatch
summary: Central bank swap lines between advanced economies function as international liquidity provision facilities that reduce funding risk for cross-border banks and put a ceiling on deviations from covered interest parity. The paper finds that more generous swap line terms encourage banks in recipient countries to increase investment in source-country currency-denominated assets, with significant effects on corporate bond prices and bank equity returns.

title: Liquidity resilience in the UK gilt futures market: evidence from the order book
central_concepts: Gilt market; Market liquidity; Liquidity preparedness
summary: The paper analyses liquidity resilience in the UK gilt futures market using high-frequency order book data from end-2014 to mid-April 2017. It finds that liquidity is resilient to external shocks including Asset Purchase Facility auctions, the Swiss franc de-peg, and the EU referendum, with no deterioration in liquidity during normal times and no trade-off between resilience and normal-time liquidity provision.

title: The deeds of speed: an agent-based model of market liquidity and flash episodes
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity; Market dysfunction; Procyclicality
summary: This paper develops an agent-based model of a limit order book market to examine how high-frequency trading contributes to flash episodes. The model shows that flash episodes arise when high-frequency traders with procyclical strategies trade significantly faster than lower-frequency participants, and that circuit breakers can reduce their frequency and magnitude.

title: Repo market functioning: the role of capital regulation
central_concepts: Repo markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: This paper shows that the leverage ratio affects repo intermediation by dealers, particularly reducing liquidity to small clients. Using a UK regulatory change that intensified the leverage ratio requirement in January 2017, the authors find that affected dealers reduced repo volumes substantially, with non-affected foreign dealers stepping in to partially offset the decline through existing relationships.

title: Would macroprudential regulation have prevented the last crisis?
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Leverage; Liquidity mismatch; Credit to the real economy; Financial stability risk; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: The paper examines whether modern macroprudential regulatory frameworks could have prevented or substantially dampened the 2008 global financial crisis, focusing on two key vulnerabilities: leverage and short-term funding at non-bank financial intermediaries, and build-up in household indebtedness. The authors find that a regulator modelled on the UK's FPC would have had better tools and mandate than the US FSOC, but both would have faced significant challenges in identifying vulnerabilities in real-time and acting aggressively, particularly in regulating loosely-regulated non-bank institutions.

title: OTC premia
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Central counterparties
summary: Using transaction-level trade repository data, the paper finds substantial and persistent heterogeneity in interest rate swap prices in the post-crisis regulatory regime. Non-CCP (bilateral) contracts command an 8 basis point premium over CCP-cleared equivalents, which decreases with initial margin posting and counterparty creditworthiness, reflecting dealers passing regulatory costs to clients through valuation adjustments (XVA).

title: Repo Market Functioning: The Role of Capital Regulation
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Repo markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Bank–non-bank linkages; Dealers and market makers
summary: Using transaction-level supervisory data, the authors show that a tightening of the leverage ratio requirement for UK banks reduced their repo intermediation, with particularly large declines for small end-users. Foreign and unconstrained dealers partially offset this withdrawal by increasing market share, though this reliance on foreign dealers may increase instability during stress periods.

title: ‘Neither a borrower nor a lender be’: How the sterling money markets dried up
central_concepts: Money markets; Market dysfunction; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: Sterling money markets experienced severe dysfunction during the 2008 financial crisis as counterparty uncertainty caused lenders to withdraw, reducing volumes and lengthening maturity mismatches, with recovery dependent on massive central bank liquidity provision. The post-crisis period saw permanent shifts in market structure and participants' liquidity management practices, with money markets remaining smaller and more reliant on secured funding than before.

title: What drives UK defined benefit pension funds’ investment behaviour?
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Procyclicality; Asset allocation
summary: The paper develops a structural model of UK defined benefit pension fund asset allocation calibrated to aggregate and cohort-level data. It finds that pension funds' responses to funding ratio shocks depend critically on sponsor financial strength: weaker-sponsored funds reduce equities when funding ratios deteriorate, while stronger-sponsored funds increase equities; all funds increase bond holdings when funding ratios improve, potentially providing countercyclical support to bond markets.

title: Macroprudential margins: a new countercyclical tool?
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Margin and collateral calls; Procyclical margin; Fire sales
summary: The paper quantifies fire-sale externalities in derivatives markets arising from procyclical margin calls and evaluates macroprudential policy tools—including quantity-based buffers and price-based taxes—to mitigate them. A countercyclical macroprudential buffer on initial margin, released flexibly in response to collateral calls, can substantially reduce or eliminate the externality across the financial cycle.

title: A balancing act: the case for macroprudential margin requirements
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Margin and collateral calls; Fire sales; Procyclical margin
summary: The authors model how macroprudential initial margin buffers on derivatives could reduce fire-sale externalities by forcing investors to hold more liquid assets, but find that achieving this requires precise calibration and comprehensive market information; even well-designed simple rules perform nearly as well, yet calibration errors risk making the system worse off than without policy.

title: How large is the leveraged loan market?
central_concepts: Private credit and private equity
summary: The leveraged loan market is approximately US$2.2 trillion when including smaller, less liquid loans and bank-held facilities, significantly larger than the commonly cited US$1.3 trillion figure based on indexed loans. Around 45% of leveraged loans are held through CLOs and 30% by investment funds and insurers, making leveraged loans comparable in size to pre-crisis US subprime mortgages relative to their credit market.

title: Who invests in securitisations of leveraged loans?
central_concepts: Private credit and private equity; Open-ended funds; Fire sales; Liquidity mismatch
summary: UK and global banks hold significant exposures to collateralised loan obligations (CLOs), securitisations of leveraged loans, with Asian investors particularly active in the market. Open-ended funds investing in riskier CLO tranches create fire-sale risk because they face redemption pressure from investors withdrawing at short notice, though regulatory standards have improved since the financial crisis.

title: Currency mispricing and dealer balance sheets
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Leverage; FX and FX swap markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Covered interest rate parity
summary: The paper finds that dealer banks with higher leverage ratios charge larger premiums for synthetic dollar funding in FX derivatives markets, breaking down covered interest rate parity. Using contract-level transaction data, the authors estimate that a one standard deviation increase in the leverage ratio raises the dollar funding cost by up to 28 basis points annually, representing an unintended consequence of post-crisis financial regulation.

title: The impact of corporate QE on liquidity: evidence from the UK
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Market liquidity
summary: The Bank of England's Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme (CBPS) in 2016–2017 improved liquidity in purchased sterling corporate bonds, as measured by reduced spreads, increased trade sizes, and lower price impact. Using granular auction-level data to control for reverse causality, the authors find robust evidence across multiple liquidity measures that central bank purchases had positive effects on market functioning, though impacts did not persist after the scheme ended.

title: Bitesize: Trading activity during the Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme
authors: David Mallaburn; Matt Roberts-Sklar; Laura Silvestri
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Dealers and market makers; Insurers; Open-ended funds
summary: This analysis of transaction-level data from the Bank of England's 2016 Corporate Bond Purchase Scheme shows that insurance companies and asset managers were the ultimate sellers of over half the bonds purchased by the central bank, with dealers intermediating these sales. The finding reveals how non-bank financial institutions responded to the policy by shifting from net buyers at announcement to net sellers during the scheme.

title: Taking regulation seriously: fire sales under solvency and liquidity constraints
central_concepts: Fire sales; Leverage; Liquidity mismatch
summary: The paper develops a quantitative model of fire sales that incorporates post-crisis regulatory constraints on banks, including risk-weighted capital, leverage, and liquidity coverage ratios. It finds that severe funding shocks generate larger fire-sale losses than solvency shocks, and that banks' ability to use liquid asset buffers and the design of leverage ratio rules significantly affect the magnitude of losses.

title: The Great War and the Bank of England as Market Maker of Last Resort
authors: Mike Anson; David Bholat; Mark Billings; Miao Kang; Ryland Thomas
central_concepts: Market maker of last resort; Money markets; Market liquidity
summary: The Bank of England acted as a market maker of last resort during the 1914 financial crisis, purchasing bills of exchange and later providing advances to accepting houses when the London money market froze following the outbreak of World War 1. This precedent demonstrates that central bank market-making interventions were not invented during the 2007-09 financial crisis but have deep historical roots in managing financial stability.

title: Decomposing changes in the functioning of the sterling repo market
central_concepts: Repo markets; Dealers and market makers; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Market liquidity
summary: Using a structural VAR model with sign restrictions, the paper finds that changes in gilt repo market functioning between 2014 and 2018 were driven primarily by changes in dealers' supply of intermediation rather than end-user demand. The introduction of the UK leverage ratio reduced dealers' willingness or ability to intermediate, making repo supply more inelastic and causing larger price increases and smaller volume increases in response to demand shocks, particularly for bilaterally traded transactions.

title: Currency Mispricing and Dealer Balance Sheets
authors: Gino Cenedese; Pasquale Della Corte; Tianyu Wang
central_concepts: FX and FX swap markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Leverage; Market dysfunction
summary: The authors show that dealer banks' leverage ratio constraints explain persistent deviations from covered interest parity in FX swap markets, with dealers charging higher premiums for synthetic dollar funding when leverage ratios tighten. A one standard deviation increase in leverage ratio raises dollar funding costs by up to 28 basis points annually, translating to approximately $92 billion in extra borrowing costs across the $33 trillion FX derivatives market.

title: New banking regulation: is it affecting the clearing of derivatives?
central_concepts: Leverage; Central counterparties; Derivatives markets; Dealers and market makers
summary: The leverage ratio capital requirement, introduced to enhance bank stability, has unintended consequences for derivatives clearing: it makes clearing derivatives on behalf of clients more expensive for dealer banks by requiring them to hold capital against client initial margin. Evidence from UK trade repository data shows that leverage-ratio-constrained banks reduce both the number of transactions they clear per client (by ~5%) and the number of clients they serve, particularly smaller clients, suggesting potential market access problems.

title: What happens when ‘angels fall’?
authors: Yuliya Baranova; Harry Goodacre; Jamie Semark
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Market liquidity
summary: The share of BBB-rated (lowest investment-grade) corporate bonds in sterling markets has grown dramatically, creating a large pool of securities at risk of downgrade to high-yield status. If downgrades accelerate to historical stress levels, forced sales by index funds, active funds and insurers could exceed dealer capacity to absorb them, potentially causing market dysfunction and disorderly price moves.

title: CCP porting, are there lessons to be learnt from elsewhere?
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Derivatives markets; Client porting
summary: Post-crisis clearing mandates have created challenges for transferring client positions when a clearing member defaults, as fewer dealers are willing to accept new clients due to capital constraints and concentration in the clearing landscape. The authors propose that CCPs with affiliated banks or banking licenses could temporarily settle client obligations during default scenarios, providing a bridge to preserve market functioning while clients are ported to other clearing members.

title: Regulatory effects on short-term interest rates
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Repo markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: The paper analyzes how EMIR and Basel III regulations affect short-term interest rates through the repo market, finding that mandatory CCP collateral reinvestment (EMIR) increases lending supply while Basel III leverage constraints reduce bank borrowing demand, together decreasing short-term rates and increasing market segmentation. The authors identify unintended regulatory consequences including rate dispersion, lending volume pressures, and potential impediments to monetary policy transmission.

title: Simulating stress in the UK corporate bond market: investor behaviour and asset fire-sales
authors: Baranova, Yuliya; Liu, Elliott; Shakir, Tara
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Fire sales; Open-ended funds; Dealers and market makers; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: The paper develops a simulation framework to model how major participants in the UK corporate bond market—including open-ended funds, dealers, insurers, and pension funds—amplify initial price shocks through forced asset sales driven by regulatory and contractual constraints. The magnitude of amplification depends on the shock's origin (larger for credit risk and interest-rate shocks than liquidity shocks) and agents' proximity to constraints, with dealer capacity limits potentially breached at spreads of 70–100 basis points.

title: Credit default swaps and corporate bond trading
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Corporate bond markets; Fire sales; Market liquidity; Margin and collateral calls
summary: Using regulatory data on CDS holdings and corporate bond transactions, the paper finds a positive liquidity spillover effect from CDS to corporate bond markets, with investors holding CDS positions showing 60% higher bond buying volumes. However, CDS mark-to-market losses cause fire sales in corporate bonds, with exposed investors' sell volumes three times higher and bond returns declining over 100 bps, illustrating a liquidity spiral risk in credit markets.

title: System-wide stress simulation
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Leverage; Fire sales; Insurers; Dealers and market makers
summary: The paper develops a general equilibrium model of UK market-based finance with representative agents from key financial sectors interacting in asset, repo, and derivatives markets. It identifies 'tipping points' where binding solvency and liquidity constraints amplify shocks, finding that tight leverage limits at broker-dealers and commercial banks substantially magnify stress, with life insurers playing a critical role in supporting asset prices.

title: How does the gilt curve react to demand shocks?
central_concepts: Gilt market; Asset price volatility; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: The authors analyze how demand shocks for UK government bonds, measured by auction bid-to-cover ratios, affect gilt yields and the shape of the yield curve. They find that demand shocks have persistent local effects on yields, particularly at longer maturities and during volatile market conditions, suggesting investors in longer-dated gilts have preferred habitats and are less price-sensitive.

title: Resilience of trading networks: evidence from the sterling corporate bond market
authors: Baranova, Y.; Czech, R.; Roberts-Sklar, M.
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Trading networks; Dealers and market makers; Interconnectedness and concentration; Core-periphery structure
summary: Using transaction-level FCA data on sterling corporate bonds, the authors find that trading networks exhibit a sparse core-periphery structure where dealers dominate intermediation, particularly for newly issued bonds. The market is resilient to bond downgrades but fragile to withdrawal of a small number of key dealers, who account for concentrated trading volumes.

title: Liquidity resilience in the long gilt futures market
central_concepts: Gilt market; Market liquidity
summary: The authors measure liquidity in the long gilt futures market from October 2014 to April 2017 using the Xetra liquidity measure (XLM) and find that round-trip trading costs have declined slightly over the period. Despite regulatory changes and structural market shifts, gilt futures liquidity shows resilience to market stress events, with disruptions typically reverting to normal levels within one to two days.

title: Does the reliance of principal trading firms on banks pose a risk to UK financial stability?
authors: Jack Worlidge; Gerardo Ferrara; Magda Rutkowska
central_concepts: Hedge funds; Bank–non-bank linkages; Market liquidity; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: Principal trading firms (PTFs) are prevalent providers of short-term liquidity in fast markets but concentrate their clearing relationships with a small number of banks, creating potential nodes of disruption. However, this concentration does not currently pose a significant risk to UK financial stability because PTFs' largest participants use diverse clearing providers and alternative access routes exist.

title: Does liquidity spill over in the credit market? The case of CDS and corporate bonds
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Corporate bond markets; Market liquidity; Liquidity spillovers
summary: CDS markets generate a positive liquidity spillover to corporate bonds, with investors holding CDS positions showing 60% higher bond trading volumes and providing countercyclical support around rating downgrades. However, losses on CDS positions can force fire sales of bonds that depress prices by over 100 basis points, creating risks of liquidity spirals in credit markets.

title: Securities settlement fails network and buy-in strategies
central_concepts: Gilt market; Market dysfunction; Interconnectedness and concentration; Buy-in process
summary: The paper examines determinants of settlement fails in UK gilts and equities, analyzes network structures of cascading fails, and develops an algorithm to identify optimal buy-in strategies to resolve chains of fails. Settlement fails can propagate through daisy chains and cause gridlock, with implications for market liquidity and systemic stability.

title: Credit easing versus quantitative easing: evidence from corporate and government bond purchase programs
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Corporate bond markets; Gilt market
summary: Using security-level data on Bank of England gilt and corporate bond purchases, the authors find that quantitative easing (QE) has significant cross-asset supply effects on corporate bond prices, with larger longer-run than short-run effects, but primarily affects the default-free component of corporate yields. Credit easing (CE) through direct corporate bond purchases is more effective than QE in reducing credit spreads and stimulating corporate bond issuance, especially for higher-rated bonds, suggesting CE could be a valuable monetary policy tool in low-interest-rate environments.

title: Liquidity transformation, collateral assets and counterparties
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Liquidity mismatch; Collateral and safe assets
summary: This paper investigates how counterparty characteristics and collateral types interact with demand for central bank liquidity in Bank of England facilities (ILTR and FLS) from 2010 to 2016. The authors find that participation reflects appropriate liquidity needs rather than moral hazard, with safer counterparties using ILTR and riskier counterparties pre-positioning but not drawing more FLS funding, suggesting central banks can provide liquidity transformation without undue balance-sheet risk.

title: OTC microstructure in a period of stress: a multi-layered network approach
central_concepts: FX and FX swap markets; Market liquidity; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Market dysfunction
summary: This paper analyses the microstructure of the FX OTC derivatives market during the January 2015 Swiss franc shock using transaction-level data and network topology. It finds a multi-layered market structure where central clients accessed liquidity more readily than peripheral participants, and dealers with loss-making positions withdrew from the market, creating a supply-driven liquidity shortage.

title: Simulating liquidity stress in the derivatives market
authors: Paddrik et al. (2020) and others working on derivatives market stress
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Margin and collateral calls; Central counterparties; Liquidity mismatch
summary: The paper simulates variation margin calls on derivative counterparties during a severe stress scenario and finds that while liquidity shortfalls would occur, they amount to only a modest fraction of daily repo market borrowing. The authors develop a model accounting for realistic payment sequencing and institutions' behaviour under liquidity constraints, identifying both 'domino' contagion effects and avoidable coordination failures in payment networks.

title: Bitesize: What might pension funds do when bond yields fall?
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Gilt market
summary: The paper models how defined-benefit pension funds respond to falling bond yields, finding that most funds de-risk by moving into bonds as deficits widen, especially those with weaker corporate sponsors. This procyclical behaviour could amplify initial yield falls through increased bond purchases.

title: Does accepting a broader set of collateral in central bank operations incentivise the use of riskier collateral by riskier counterparties?
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Collateral and safe assets; Financial stability risk
summary: The authors investigate whether the Bank of England's acceptance of a broad range of collateral in liquidity operations incentivises riskier counterparties to hold riskier assets. Using a quasi-natural experiment comparing the ILTR and FLS facilities from 2010–2016, they find no evidence that weaker banks concentrate in riskier collateral; instead, collateral use patterns reflect the intended incentives of each operation's fee and maturity structure.

title: Margin call! Cash shortfall?
authors: Marco Bardoscia; Gerardo Ferrara; Nicholas Vause
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Derivatives markets
summary: The authors simulate stress-scenario margin calls on derivative market participants and assess whether money markets could absorb the resulting borrowing demand. They find that even in a severe scenario generating $300 billion in margin calls, the resulting $54 billion borrowing requirement would be less than 10% of average daily international repo borrowing, suggesting money markets could accommodate the demand.

title: Have hedge funds increased their use of repo borrowing?
central_concepts: Hedge funds; Repo markets
summary: Survey data show that hedge funds significantly increased their repo borrowing in 2019, with cash borrowed rising 41% between October 2018 and April 2019. This increased demand for repo funding by hedge funds may have contributed to volatility in the US dollar repo market.

title: Crossing the credit channel: credit spreads and firm heterogeneity
central_concepts: Leverage; Corporate bond markets; Monetary policy transmission via markets; Dealers and market makers
summary: Credit spreads rise more sharply for highly leveraged firms after monetary policy tightening, with most of the increase driven by a risk premium component unrelated to default risk. The results indicate that frictions in financial intermediation sector play a crucial role in transmitting monetary policy to firm borrowing costs.

title: How have firms’ views on financial stability risks in the UK changed over the past decade?
authors: Ryan Lovelock; Icaro Rebolledo; Lyndsey Pereira-Brereton
central_concepts: Financial stability risk
summary: The Bank of England's Systemic Risk Survey tracks how market participants' views on financial stability risks have evolved over the past decade. While firms' concerns shifted from financial crises and market disruption in 2008-2009 to political, geopolitical and cyber risks by 2015-2020, their overall confidence in the UK financial system remained high throughout.

title: Quality is our asset: the international transmission of liquidity regulation
central_concepts: Margin policy reforms; Bank–non-bank linkages; Collateral and safe assets; Gilt market
summary: This paper examines how UK banks adjust their cross-border lending in response to changes in liquidity regulation (Individual Liquidity Guidance), finding that a 1 percentage point increase in liquidity requirements reduces external lending growth by around 0.6 percentage points. The impact varies significantly by bank nationality and deposit funding: foreign subsidiaries from non-HQLA-issuing countries cut lending most sharply, while UK banks with retail deposit bases can offset the effect by shifting to sovereign debt holdings.

title: Informed trading in government bond markets
authors: Informed trading in government bond markets - Bank of England Working Paper 2020
central_concepts: Gilt market; Hedge funds; Money market funds; Informed trading
summary: Using comprehensive FCA regulatory data on all gilt market transactions, the authors find that hedge funds' daily trading positively predicts gilt returns over 1–5 days before reversing, while mutual funds' trading predicts returns over 1–2 months with no reversal. Hedge funds profit by trading ahead of other investors' demand, while mutual funds profit from forecasting changes in short-term interest rates.

title: What role did margin play during the Covid-19 shock?
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Derivatives markets
summary: Margin calls in derivatives markets surged during the March 2020 Covid-19 shock, with variation margin reaching five times normal levels and initial margin requirements rising 31%, contributing to a system-wide dash for cash. The paper argues that prudent margining is essential for managing counterparty risk and that market participants must ensure their liquidity strategies account for the possibility of large margin calls during stress.

title: Modelling fire sale contagion across banks and non-banks
central_concepts: Fire sales; Interconnectedness and concentration; Market-based finance; Open-ended funds
summary: The paper models fire sale contagion across UK banks and non-bank financial institutions through commonly held assets, finding that ignoring cross-sector asset holdings underestimates fire sale losses by 47% on average. It shows fire sale losses from asset liquidations typically exceed direct losses from initial shocks, and that liquidation strategy significantly affects both aggregate systemic losses and spillover effects across sectors.

title: Dollar shortages and central bank swap lines
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Bank–non-bank linkages; Credit to the real economy
summary: The paper develops a macroeconomic model showing that 'dollar shortage' shocks—sudden declines in foreign currency funding for non-US banks—significantly contract lending, investment and output through balance sheet mismatches and exchange rate depreciation. Central bank swap lines can substantially attenuate these effects if deployed at sufficient scale, as demonstrated through calibration to Korea's experience during the Covid-19 pandemic.

title: The macro consequences of dollar shortages and central bank swap lines during the Covid-19 pandemic
central_concepts: Money markets; FX and FX swap markets; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: Dollar shortages in offshore funding markets during the Covid-19 pandemic reduced dollar availability and raised borrowing costs for non-US financial systems, leading to exchange rate depreciation and bank lending contractions. Central bank swap lines between the Federal Reserve and foreign central banks reduced these negative macroeconomic effects by about 20% by channelling dollars to domestic banking systems.

title: What sources of credit do UK companies rely on?
authors: Marek Rojicek; Leo Fernandes; Ashley Young; Varun Paul; Oliver Thew; Miriam Kurtosiova; Richard Button; David Baumslag
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Dealers and market makers; Credit to the real economy
summary: UK companies' reliance on credit sources varies by size: smaller firms depend primarily on banks, while larger companies access both bank lending and market-based funding through capital markets. The document surveys these funding patterns during the Covid-19 crisis, when UK companies faced a substantial aggregate cash-flow deficit of around £140 billion, highlighting the importance of both banking and capital market sources in providing credit to businesses.

title: Covid-19 briefing: cross-border dollar funding
central_concepts: Money market funds; Run risk; FX and FX swap markets; Covered interest rate parity; Central bank backstop facilities; Bank–non-bank linkages
summary: During the Covid-19 pandemic, stress in US dollar money markets dried up funding for non-US banks as prime money market funds experienced large outflows and FX swap spreads widened sharply. The Federal Reserve's expansion of swap lines with foreign central banks helped restore functioning by providing an alternative source of dollar funding and anchoring the price of synthetic dollar financing.

title: Informed trading in government bond markets
authors: Robert Czech; Shiyang Huang; Dong Lou; Tianyu Wang
central_concepts: Hedge funds; Open-ended funds; Gilt market; Information asymmetry
summary: Using comprehensive regulatory trading data from the UK gilt market, the authors show that hedge funds and mutual funds possess information advantages and earn abnormal returns, operating through different strategies: hedge funds predict mutual fund order flows over days to weeks, while mutual funds predict interest rate changes over months. Both earn higher returns on macroeconomic announcement days, suggesting they are better at processing public information relevant to government bond pricing.

title: Why do firms need to accelerate the transition from Libor benchmarks?
central_concepts: Money markets
summary: Libor, a key interest rate benchmark for trillions of pounds of financial contracts, is becoming unreliable due to declining transaction volumes since the financial crisis and will be discontinued after end-2021. During the March 2020 Covid-19 market stress, Libor's weakness was exposed when underlying market activity collapsed and rates became determined almost entirely by bank expert judgment, while the alternative benchmark SONIA remained robust and closely tracked Bank Rate.

title: Market fragility in the pandemic era
authors: Gerardo Ferrara; Maria Flora; Roberto Renò
central_concepts: Market dysfunction; Flash crashes; Dash for cash
summary: The paper develops a new econometric methodology based on drift statistics to detect market fragility and dysfunction in financial markets, particularly flash crashes and V-shaped price distortions. Applied to sovereign bond markets during the March 2020 pandemic crisis, the method identifies periods when prices diverge from fundamentals, including the flight-to-quality phase and the subsequent dash-for-cash episode.

title: Left feeling unsettled: what are settlement failures, how prevalent are they, and what do we do about them?
authors: Gary Harper; Pedro Gurrola-Perez; Jieshuang He
central_concepts: Settlement system and failures; Gilt market; Equity markets; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: Settlement failures in UK gilt and equity markets occur in 2-16% of daily trades by volume and often cascade through counterparties, creating gridlock effects that impair market functioning. The authors develop a network-based algorithm to identify cascade-driven failures and propose a centralised buy-in strategy to efficiently resolve cascades in the settlement system.

title: Financial shocks, reopening the case
central_concepts: Global shocks (US, euro area, Japan); Credit to the real economy; Corporate bond markets; Private credit and private equity
summary: The paper proposes a method to identify financial shocks by examining the relative movements of loan and bond financing, finding that financial shocks account for around a third of US business cycle fluctuations and are predictive of corporate bond spreads. The approach uses a DSGE model incorporating firms' debt arbitrage between loans and bonds to isolate credit supply disturbances from other economic shocks.

title: Informed trading and the dynamics of client-dealer connections in corporate bond markets
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Dealers and market makers; Informed trading
summary: Using regulatory data with disclosed counterparty identities, the paper shows that clients in corporate bond markets achieve higher trading performance when trading with more dealers, with stronger effects for informationally sensitive clients and assets. The effect is stronger and more persistent in corporate bonds than government bonds, consistent with an information-based mechanism where informed traders split orders across multiple dealers to conceal private information.

title: The central bank balance sheet as a policy tool: past, present and future
authors: Andrew Bailey; Jonathan Bridges; Richard Harrison; Josh Jones; Aakash Mankodi
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Market dysfunction; Gilt market
summary: The paper examines lessons from a decade of quantitative easing and the central bank response to the Covid-19 crisis, finding that large QE programmes implemented rapidly are particularly effective during market dysfunction. It argues that QE's effectiveness depends on state-contingent factors and the source of liquidity demand, with implications for future central bank balance sheet policies and operational frameworks.

title: How does the repo market behave under stress? Evidence from the Covid-19 crisis
central_concepts: Repo markets; Dash for cash
summary: Using granular transaction-level data from the overnight gilt repo market including the Covid-19 crisis, the paper applies network analysis to show how repo market structure and behaviour change under stress. Key findings include increased volumes in cleared markets as dealers prefer netting benefits, decreased funding to most non-banks except hedge funds, and significantly higher spreads when core sectors lend to the periphery, reflecting dealers' balance-sheet constraints from regulatory leverage limits.

title: What to expect when they’re expecting
authors: Maren Froemel; Mike Joyce; Iryna Kaminska
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Gilt market; Market liquidity
summary: The authors analyse high-frequency gilt market reactions to QE announcements in 2020, finding that yield responses were broadly proportional to market surprises about the expected medium-term stock of QE purchases. They identify multiple transmission channels including local supply effects, signalling effects on future policy rates, and liquidity premium effects, particularly during the acute stress in March 2020.

title: Decomposing changes in the functioning of the sterling repo market from 2014 to 2018
central_concepts: Repo markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Margin policy reforms
summary: The paper decomposes changes in sterling gilt repo market functioning from 2014 to 2018 using a structural vector autoregression model, finding that fluctuations in repo spreads were driven primarily by changes in dealers' supply of intermediation. The authors conclude that the introduction of the UK leverage ratio in 2016 may have reduced dealers' willingness to accommodate demand for cash, particularly for non-nettable bilateral transactions, making repo markets less elastic to demand shocks.
