title: Procyclicality mechanisms in the financial system: what we know and some open questions
authors: Robert Czech; Simon Jurkatis; Arjun Mahalingam; Laura Silvestri; Nick Vause
central_concepts: Procyclicality; Margin and collateral calls; Procyclical margin; Open-ended funds; Hedge funds; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: The paper reviews four key procyclicality mechanisms in financial markets—margin calls on derivatives, fund redemptions, hedge fund deleveraging, and dealer intermediation constraints—that amplified the economic downturn during the Covid-19 crisis. It identifies research gaps on the strength of these mechanisms and potential policy mitigations such as anti-procyclicality measures, fund liquidity tools, and market structure reforms.

title: Could price data from exchange-traded funds help open-ended fund managers calculate price adjustments?
central_concepts: Open-ended funds; Liquidity mismatch; Run risk
summary: Open-ended funds may not fully reflect the true cost of liquidating assets in their swing pricing adjustments. ETF price data, such as bid-ask spreads and NAV discounts, could help OEF managers calculate more accurate price adjustments, especially during market stress like March 2020.

title: Did movements in exchange-traded funds act as a price signal for open-ended fund investors during the ‘dash for cash’ stress period?
central_concepts: Open-ended funds; Dash for cash; Corporate bond markets
summary: During the March 2020 'dash for cash', ETF NAV discounts provided predictive information about next-day movements in open-ended fund (OEF) NAVs, suggesting that OEF valuations were slower to incorporate price information than ETFs. In normal conditions, no such relationship existed, but during stress, a 1% ETF NAV discount predicted a 0.28% negative change in expected OEF NAV movements, which could amplify run risk if investors anticipate stale valuations.

title: Preferred habitat investors in the UK government bond market
authors: Julia Giese; Michael Joyce; Jack Meaning; Jack Worlidge
central_concepts: Preferred habitat investors; Gilt market; LDI funds and pension schemes; Central bank backstop facilities; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: Using granular transaction-level data on the UK gilt market, the authors identify distinct investor groups exhibiting preferred habitat behaviour through cluster analysis, finding that institutional investors like pension funds and life insurers show lower price sensitivity and higher portfolio duration stability than other investors. The paper provides evidence that these preferred habitat investors sold relatively more gilt holdings to the Bank of England during QE4 (August 2016–March 2017), consistent with the portfolio balance channel of monetary transmission.

title: I need a dollar, dollar, a dollar is what I need
central_concepts: Dash for cash; Corporate bond markets; US Treasury market
summary: The paper shows that during the March 2020 Covid crisis, corporate bond spreads increased more for dollar-denominated bonds and short-maturity dollar bonds, but long-maturity non-dollar bonds, suggesting investors experienced a 'dash for dollars' rather than a general dash for cash. The authors attribute this to the US dollar's role as a dominant currency in the international monetary and financial system, creating particular dollar funding needs during stress.

title: No economy is an island: how foreign shocks affect UK macrofinancial stability
central_concepts: Global shocks (US, euro area, Japan); Bank–non-bank linkages
summary: The paper quantifies how foreign shocks transmit to the UK economy through trade and financial channels, finding that global developments explain about half of UK GDP variation and almost all financial conditions variation from 1997–2019. Foreign developments also drive over two-thirds of variation in UK tail risk (severe downside outcomes), with particular emphasis on vulnerabilities in non-bank financial intermediation exposed during Covid-19.

title: How have firms’ views on financial stability risks changed since the Covid pandemic?
central_concepts: Financial stability risk; Cyber risk
summary: The Bank of England's Systemic Risk Survey tracks how market participants' views on financial stability risks have evolved over the past decade and since Covid-19. Cyber attacks, pandemic risks, and geopolitical risks have become the most frequently cited threats to the UK financial system, replacing political risk as the dominant concern.

title: A CBA of APC: analysing approaches to procyclicality reduction in CCP initial margin models
authors: Murphy et al.; Bank of England staff
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Margin and collateral calls; Procyclical margin; Procyclicality; Margin policy reforms
summary: The paper develops a cost-benefit framework to quantify the trade-offs between reducing procyclicality in CCP margin models and the cost of higher average margin requirements. Large margin calls in March 2020 prompted reassessment of how CCPs should set initial margin to reduce liquidity strains while maintaining adequate risk coverage.

title: An unintended consequence of holding dollar assets
central_concepts: Gilt market; FX and FX swap markets; Margin and collateral calls; Insurers; LDI funds and pension schemes
summary: The paper examines UK gilt market trading during the March 2020 COVID crisis, finding that insurance companies and pension funds sold £3.8bn of gilts. The authors show this selling was driven by margin calls on their USD FX hedging positions as the dollar appreciated, revealing how the dollar's reserve currency status can amplify domestic government bond market stress.

title: Not bound, but still relevant: How does the leverage ratio affect banks’ intermediation?
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Repo markets; Banks' internal capital allocation
summary: The paper shows that banks not bound by the leverage ratio requirement still reduce repo intermediation because they apply the leverage ratio internally at the business-unit level rather than only at the consolidated level as legally required. This practice causes repo to bear disproportionate leverage costs relative to risk-weighted capital costs, discouraging repo investment even when the leverage ratio does not constrain the bank overall.

title: The repo market under Basel III
central_concepts: Repo markets; Margin and collateral calls; Leverage; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: This paper uses proprietary Bank of England repo transaction data to assess how Basel III regulatory ratios (leverage, capital, and liquidity coverage) affect UK repo market dynamics, pricing, volumes, and microstructure. The authors find non-uniform effects across ratios and participants, including a substitution of bank borrowing from dealers to investment funds, increased CCP participation, and greater activity reductions under stress for multiply-constrained banks, raising questions about market fragility and regulatory spillovers.

title: The costs and benefits of reducing the cyclicality of margin models
central_concepts: Procyclical margin; Margin and collateral calls
summary: The paper proposes a cost-benefit framework for assessing strategies to reduce the procyclicality of margin requirements in derivative markets, using two metrics (large-call and peak-to-trough) to measure benefits against average collateral costs. It finds that model recalibration and cap tools can substantially reduce procyclicality at relatively low cost, and recommends outcome-based regulation allowing clearing houses flexibility in choosing least-cost mitigation strategies.

title: Preferred habitat behaviour in the gilt market
authors: Julia Giese; Michael Joyce; Jack Meaning; Jack Worlidge
central_concepts: Gilt market; Central bank backstop facilities; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: Using granular Euroclear data on gilt holdings and trades, the authors identify investor groups with strong preferences for specific maturity segments through clustering analysis, including foreign central banks, pension funds and insurers. They show these preferred habitat investors are less price-sensitive than arbitrageurs and trace their disproportionate role as sellers to the Bank of England's QE4 purchases between August 2016 and March 2017, providing evidence for the portfolio rebalancing channel of QE.

title: An unintended consequence of holding dollar assets
authors: Robert Czech; Shiyang Huang; Dong Lou; Tianyu Wang
central_concepts: Insurers; FX and FX swap markets; Margin and collateral calls; Gilt market; Fire sales; Dash for cash
summary: The paper identifies a mechanism through which the dollar's reserve currency status amplified the March 2020 gilt market stress: UK insurers and pension funds hedged large dollar asset holdings through FX derivatives, and when the dollar appreciated sharply, margin calls on these positions forced them to sell gilts, raising yields by up to 30 basis points. The authors argue this reveals an unintended consequence of currency hedging and call for enhanced liquidity preparedness and more predictable margin frameworks in the ICPF sector.

title: Collateral cycles
authors: Gai, Prasanna; Gale, Douglas; Gambacorta, Leonardo; Gurrieri, Marco; Hacioglu Hoke, Sezen; Koulischer, Felix; Mandal, Kaushik; Ranaldo, Angelo; Salakhova, Diana
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Repo markets; Margin and collateral calls; Procyclical margin; Collateral and safe assets
summary: Using supervisory data from UK CCPs, the paper documents persistent collateral cycles where cash flows between financial markets and CCPs as clearing members borrow in repo to meet procyclical margin requirements (onward phase), and CCPs invest collected cash back into reverse repos and bonds (backward phase). The analysis shows that CCP margin requirements and repo market activity comove procyclically with volatility, and that both phases significantly affect repo rates with important implications for financial stability.

title: Information chasing versus adverse selection
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Adverse selection risk; Information asymmetry
summary: This paper shows that in over-the-counter financial markets, dealers compete to execute informed orders by offering better pricing, contrary to classic adverse selection theory, because executing informed trades allows dealers to extract information to improve future quotes. Using trade-level data from the UK government bond market, the authors find that more informed clients receive lower trading costs in cross-client comparisons, while within-client comparisons show informed trades receive worse pricing.

title: Size discount and size penalty: trading costs in bond markets
central_concepts: Gilt market; Corporate bond markets; Market liquidity; Dealers and market makers; Trading costs
summary: The paper shows that larger trades in government bond markets obtain lower trading costs when comparing across different traders ('size discount'), but face higher costs within the same trader over time ('size penalty'). The size penalty is larger for corporate bonds, during macroeconomic surprises and Covid-19, and is substantially smaller in US Treasuries than UK gilts, suggesting information asymmetry and market structure play important roles in determining trading costs.

title: Predicting exchange rates
authors: Robert Czech; Pasquale Della Corte; Shiyang Huang; Tianyu Wang
central_concepts: FX and FX swap markets; Derivatives markets; Market liquidity
summary: Using granular FX option trade data from 2014-2016, the authors show that higher trading volumes in FX options predict foreign currency depreciation the next day, particularly around US macroeconomic announcements and for options with high embedded leverage. Hedge funds and real money investors demonstrate superior predictive ability, suggesting informed traders incorporate information into prices and accelerate price discovery in FX markets.

title: Comparing search and intermediation frictions across markets
authors: authors not explicitly listed in document
central_concepts: Gilt market; Corporate bond markets; Dealers and market makers; Search frictions; Intermediation frictions
summary: The paper develops a structural search-and-bargaining model of OTC trading to estimate frictions and welfare losses in UK government and corporate bond markets using transaction-level data. Welfare losses are 2.4% in government bonds and 5.0% in corporate bonds during normal times, driven primarily by search delays rather than intermediation frictions, but these losses more than double during COVID-19 stress, revealing fragility in the OTC market structure.

title: Reducing liquidity mismatch in open‑ended funds: a cost-benefit analysis
central_concepts: Open-ended funds; Liquidity mismatch; Fund liquidity management tools
summary: The paper conducts a cost-benefit analysis of swing pricing in UK corporate bond open-ended funds (OEFs) to reduce liquidity mismatch. Using empirical flow-performance regressions, a fund-dealer model, and GDP at risk estimates, the authors find that greater swing pricing use could reduce amplification of corporate bond spread shocks by around 8% and improve GDP tail risk, with likely net financial stability benefits.

title: Central bank swap lines: micro-level evidence
authors: Bahaj, Arpad; Mallick, Sohit; Reis, Ricardo
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Derivatives markets; Basis trades
summary: Using transaction-level data from the Bank of England, this paper shows that central bank dollar swap lines during the March 2020 Covid crisis reduced pricing inefficiencies in FX forward and swap markets, particularly for non-dealer customers, by lowering covered interest parity deviations. The mechanism is one of demand substitution: dealers use cheaper swap line funding to replace expensive synthetic dollar funding through FX swaps rather than expanding arbitrage activity.

title: A structural model of liquidity in over‑the‑counter markets
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Market liquidity; Dealers and market makers; Over-the-counter markets
summary: Using detailed data on sterling corporate bond trading, the authors build a structural search model showing that just 8% of traders supply as much liquidity as the remaining 92%, making markets highly vulnerable to shocks to these key traders. Bank capital regulation reduces dealer willingness to hold assets and liquidity, though endogenous trader responses mitigate welfare costs by 30%; trading platforms would improve aggregate welfare but harm the most active traders, explaining their slow adoption.

title: The local supply channel of QE: evidence from the Bank of England’s gilt purchases
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Gilt market; Market liquidity
summary: The paper analyses the importance of the 'local supply' channel—whereby central bank purchases create scarcity in purchased securities, raising prices and lowering yields—across all five Bank of England QE programmes from 2009 to 2020. It finds strong evidence for local supply effects on gilt yields both at announcements and after purchases begin, with the largest impact in QE1 (2009) that diminished over subsequent rounds, suggesting other transmission channels gained relative importance.

title: QE at the Bank of England: a perspective on its functioning and effectiveness
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Gilt market; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: This article reviews evidence on how quantitative easing (QE) transmits to the UK economy, finding that QE announcements lower gilt yields through multiple channels including signalling, portfolio balance, liquidity, market functioning, and uncertainty effects. The paper concludes that QE has supported monetary policy objectives by lowering interest rates and borrowing costs, with effects varying significantly across different economic circumstances and programme episodes.

title: What drives repo haircuts? Evidence from the UK market
authors: Christian Julliard; Gábor Pintér; Karamfil Todorov; Jean-Charles Wijnandts; Kathy Yuan
central_concepts: Repo markets; Margin and collateral calls; Bank–non-bank linkages; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: Using transaction-level UK repo data, the authors document that only 61% of bilateral repos use high-quality collateral and find that counterparty characteristics, collateral quality, and relationship lending are the primary drivers of haircuts, with information frictions playing a central role rather than lenders' liquidity or default risk. Banks intermediate liquidity across counterparties and use central clearing counterparties to reallocate high-quality collateral, with haircut spreads ranging from 30 basis points to 1.3% reflecting intermediation margins.

title: Links between government bond and futures markets: dealer-client relationships and price discovery in the UK
authors: Anderson, Webber, Noss, Beale and Crowley-Reidy (2015) implied, though primary authors not explicitly listed in abstract
central_concepts: Gilt market; Derivatives markets; Dealers and market makers; Central counterparties
summary: This paper analyses the resilience of UK gilt cash and futures markets by studying dealer-client trading and clearing relationships using granular transaction data, and examines how price discovery occurs between these two markets. The authors find that trading and clearing activity are concentrated among a few key dealers, particularly firms that are both GEMMs and clearing members, and that order flows from certain client sectors in futures markets affect cash market prices.

title: Rolling substitutions in financial markets: did quantitative easing in 2020 lead to portfolio rebalancing?
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Monetary policy transmission via markets; Gilt market; LDI funds and pension schemes; Corporate bond markets
summary: Using granular MiFID II transaction data from 2018–2020, the paper finds evidence that insurance companies and pension funds (ICPFs) reduced their net purchases of newly issued gilts during QE5 in 2020 and increased investment in corporate bonds, consistent with a portfolio rebalancing channel of QE. The estimated substitution effect suggests that for every £1 billion of foregone gilt investment, ICPFs invested approximately £180 million more in investment-grade corporate bonds.

title: Cryptoassets, the metaverse and systemic risk
central_concepts: Stablecoins and crypto; Open-ended funds; Leverage; Financial stability risk
summary: The paper argues that cryptoassets could play important roles in an open, decentralised metaverse by enabling interoperable digital ownership and aligning incentives in decentralised networks. If the metaverse grows significantly, existing risks from cryptoassets—including price volatility, leverage, stablecoin runs, and smart contract vulnerabilities—could scale to systemic financial stability consequences through non-bank holdings, fire sales, and bank exposures.

title: Back to the Future IV: challenges for financial stability policy in the next decade
authors: Alina Barnett; Sinem Hacioglu Hoke; Simon Lloyd
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Data and transparency on non-banks; Macroprudential policy for non-banks; Financial stability risk
summary: The paper identifies three emerging financial stability challenges: non-bank financial intermediation, cryptoassets and DeFi, and climate change, all of which require macroprudential frameworks but face common obstacles of limited data, international coordination needs, and unclear optimal resilience levels. The 2020 dash for cash is highlighted as demonstrating vulnerabilities in market-based finance that policymakers must address through dynamic toolkits and granular monitoring.

title: Swing or amiss: are fund pricing rules good for financial stability?
central_concepts: Open-ended funds; Liquidity mismatch; Corporate bond markets; Procyclicality; Fund liquidity management tools
summary: The paper finds that enhanced swing pricing in open-ended funds can reduce amplification of shocks to corporate bond prices and improve GDP-at-risk outcomes, with modest but relevant potential macroeconomic benefits and limited costs. The analysis uses a fund-dealer model to show that swing pricing reduces procyclical asset sales by making fund flows less sensitive to performance, thereby dampening financial instability.

title: Bond supply, yield drifts, and liquidity provision before macroeconomic announcements
central_concepts: Gilt market; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Asset price volatility; Bond supply
summary: UK gilt yields rise systematically in the two days before macroeconomic announcements, particularly when bond issuance coincides with these pre-news windows, driven by higher term premia and dealer inventory constraints. The effect reflects a shift in liquidity provision away from informed hedge funds toward passive investors like foreign central banks and pension funds, which demand higher compensation for bearing the risk of buying newly issued gilts before information events.

title: The ring-fencing bonus
central_concepts: Ring-fencing; Repo markets; Bank counterparty risk
summary: Using confidential sterling repo transaction data, the authors find that ring-fenced bank subsidiaries are perceived as safer by market participants, evidenced by lower repo borrowing costs of 0.885 basis points and a pronounced safe-haven effect during stress periods like Covid-19. Ring-fencing creates measurably safer subsidiaries without harming non-ring-fenced subsidiaries, suggesting structural reforms can enhance financial stability.

title: Efficiency of central clearing under liquidity stress
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Derivatives markets; Margin and collateral calls; Collateral and safe assets
summary: This paper models how the fraction of derivatives contracts that are centrally cleared affects the aggregate demand for collateral through variation margin calls during liquidity stress. The authors find that aggregate liquidity shortfalls follow a U-shaped relationship with the degree of central clearing when institutions have different counterparties for centrally cleared versus bilateral contracts, suggesting an optimal intermediate level of clearing rather than full central clearing.

title: Stress relief? Funding structures and resilience to the Covid Shock
authors: Forbes, Kristin J.; Hjørungdal, Knut Are; Nenova, Tsvetelina; Straub, Stéphane
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Dealers and market makers; Bank–non-bank linkages; FX and FX swap markets; Market dysfunction
summary: The paper analyzes how different funding structures affected financial stress during the March 2020 Covid-19 shock, using credit default swap spreads for banks and corporates across 68 countries. It finds that banks reliant on non-bank financial institution (NBFI) funding and US dollar funding were significantly more vulnerable, while structure-specific policies targeting these vulnerabilities—particularly NBFI support and USD swap lines—were more effective than broader regulatory easing.

title: Strengthening the resilience of market-based finance
authors: Naoto Takemoto; Simon Jurkatis; Nicholas Vause
events: Archegos default; March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Money market funds; Open-ended funds; LDI funds and pension schemes; Dealers and market makers; Leverage; Margin and collateral calls; Dash for cash; Market dysfunction; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Gilt market
summary: Market-based finance has both mitigated and amplified economic effects of financial crises: it substituted for banks after the GFC but propagated a dash for cash during Covid and amplified gilt yields increases from pension fund sales. The paper outlines five aspects of MBF vulnerability—money market funds, open-ended funds, margin calls, leveraged investors, and dealer-intermediated markets—and summarizes international policy proposals to enhance resilience.

title: To what extent did the recent increase in long-term UK interest rates reflect UK-specific factors?
central_concepts: Gilt market; Asset price volatility
summary: Between January and October 2022, UK ten-year gilt yields rose by approximately 300 basis points, with two-thirds of the increase occurring since August. Using heteroskedasticity-based decomposition, the analysis finds that while global factors (shocks from the US, euro area, and Japan) drove the initial moves, UK-specific factors—including higher expected Bank Rate, political and economic uncertainty from fiscal announcements, and market illiquidity—became increasingly important drivers since August.

title: Do larger bond trades cost more to execute?
central_concepts: Gilt market; Corporate bond markets; Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity
summary: Using transaction-level data from UK bond markets 2011-17, the authors show that while larger trades receive lower costs than smaller trades overall (size discount), this reverses within individual clients (size penalty), driven by information asymmetry and inventory costs. The size penalty is larger for hedge funds and asset managers, larger during macro shocks, and larger in corporate bonds and less liquid markets, consistent with informed trading explanations.

title: ‘There is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid’: margin calls and liquidity demand in volatile commodity markets
authors: Gerardo Ferrara; Gerardo Martinez; Pelagia Neocleous; Pierre Ortlieb; Manesh Powar
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Procyclical margin; Liquidity mismatch
summary: During the 2022 commodity price spike, sharp increases in margin requirements on derivatives positions created severe liquidity pressure on non-financial commodity traders, who unlike financial institutions do not hold securities buffers and must instead borrow from banks. The resulting strains on credit lines and reduced hedging activity highlight structural vulnerabilities in how non-banks manage liquidity mismatches between margin calls and physical asset sales.

title: Negative rates, monetary policy transmission and cross-border lending via international financial centres
authors: Unspecified - Bank of England working paper authors
central_concepts: Monetary policy transmission via markets; Dealers and market makers; Bank–non-bank linkages
summary: The paper examines how negative interest rate policies (NIRP) in major economies affect the transmission of monetary policy through cross-border bank lending via international financial centres (IFCs) such as London, Hong Kong and Dublin. It finds that NIRP impairs the bank-lending channel for cross-border lending to non-bank sectors, particularly for banks with weak local deposit bases in IFCs, though this effect varies significantly with banks' funding structures and is less pronounced for interbank lending.

title: Nonbank lenders as global shock absorbers: evidence from US monetary policy spillovers
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Bank–non-bank linkages
summary: The paper finds that nonbank lenders increase international syndicated dollar lending to non-US corporates when US monetary policy tightens, while banks contract, attenuating the transmission of US monetary policy spillovers globally. This substitution is larger for riskier borrowers and emerging market firms, suggesting nonbanks have higher risk tolerance but also highlighting potential financial stability trade-offs given their greater fragility.

title: An anatomy of the 2022 gilt market crisis
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Gilt market; Repo markets; Derivatives markets; Market liquidity; Procyclical margin
summary: Using transaction-level data on gilt, repo and interest-rate swap markets, the authors document that pre-crisis derivative and repo exposures of LDI-pension-insurance firms predicted their forced gilt sales during the September-October 2022 crisis, and that illiquidity spilled over to other market segments via transaction cost increases and price dispersion. A small number of concentrated firms drove most LDI sales, while hedge funds provided modest liquidity provision timed to maximize returns.

title: The challenges of measuring financial conditions
central_concepts: Global financial conditions; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The paper proposes a UK financial conditions index (FCI) using principal component analysis on government bond yields, credit spreads, exchange rates, and equity prices to measure the ease of financing for households and firms. The index shows that financial conditions tightened significantly over the 2021–22 policy cycle, with each unit of Bank Rate increase producing more tightening than in previous cycles, though robustness checks reveal substantial uncertainty in the measurement.

title: Self-fulfilling fire sales and market backstops
central_concepts: Fire sales; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Open-ended funds; Market maker of last resort
summary: The paper develops a global games model showing that a central bank market backstop can eliminate self-fulfilling fire sales in bond markets by credibly committing to large purchases at a low discount, without needing to actually buy assets. However, if the central bank acts less aggressively than expected, funds respond by holding more bonds ('moral hazard'), increasing fire sale risk.

title: Price formation in markets with trading delays
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Trading delays; Market liquidity; Information acquisition
summary: The paper develops a theoretical model of price formation in markets with trading delays, showing that longer delays reduce traders' incentives to acquire information, thus lowering price informativeness in equilibrium. The authors validate the theory using transaction-level data from the UK corporate bond market, confirming that price efficiency decreases and price dispersion follows a non-monotonic relationship with trading delays.

title: The potential impact of broader central clearing on dealer balance sheet capacity: a case study of UK gilt and gilt repo markets
authors: Yuliya Baranova; Eleanor Holbrook; David MacDonald; William Rawstorne; Nicholas Vause; Georgia Waddington
central_concepts: Central counterparties; Dealers and market makers; Gilt market; Repo markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: The paper estimates that broader central clearing in gilt and gilt repo markets could reduce dealers' balance-sheet exposures by 40-60% through improved netting of trades, potentially boosting their aggregate leverage ratio by 3-5 basis points and allowing repo desks to expand trading capacity significantly during stress episodes like the March 2020 dash for cash. For cash gilts, central clearing would have limited impact on dealers' leverage ratios due to accounting changes implemented in January 2023, though it could reduce settlement obligations by around 50%.

title: The market for inflation risk
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Dealers and market makers; LDI funds and pension schemes; Hedge funds; Asset price volatility
summary: Using transaction-level data on UK inflation swaps, the paper identifies market segmentation with pension funds trading at long maturities and hedge funds at short maturities, with dealer banks as net sellers of inflation protection. The authors propose identification strategies to separate expected inflation from market frictions, finding that long-maturity swap prices track expected inflation reasonably well but short-maturity prices are dominated by friction-driven movements.

title: Funding structures and resilience to shocks after a decade of regulatory reform
authors: Kristin Forbes; Christian Friedrich; Dennis Reinhardt
events: March 2023 banking stress; March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Bank–non-bank linkages; FX and FX swap markets; Financial stability risk
summary: Using CDS spreads during the March 2020 Covid dash for cash, the authors find that banks and corporates reliant on funding from non-bank financial institutions and US dollar markets experienced significantly greater stress. Targeted policy interventions supporting NBFIs and providing US dollar swap lines were more effective at reducing financial stress than broader macroeconomic or banking regulatory responses.

title: Yield curve sensitivity to investor positioning around economic shocks
central_concepts: Basis trades; Asset price volatility; Derivatives markets; Investor positioning
summary: Using daily EMIR trade repository data on short sterling futures from October 2018 to January 2020, the authors investigate whether speculative investor positioning amplifies yield curve moves around economic shocks. They find limited evidence that positioning affects pricing around macroeconomic or monetary policy news, consistent with efficient market functioning, but do find that net positions influenced yield curve sensitivity to Brexit shocks, with long positions dampening and short positions amplifying the response.

title: Lifting the lid on a liquidity crisis
authors: Lydia Henning; Simon Jurkatis; Manesh Powar; Gian Valentini
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Repo markets; Gilt market; Derivatives markets; Leverage; Margin and collateral calls
summary: Using transaction-level regulatory data on the September 2022 gilt market stress, the authors quantify LDI and pension fund leverage, margin calls, and deleveraging behaviour. They find that repo was the primary source of margin calls, and that LDI funds reduced leverage through both gilt and corporate bond sales while unwinding repo positions.

title: Hedging, market concentration and monetary policy: a joint analysis of gilt and derivatives exposures
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Gilt market; Derivatives markets; LDI funds and pension schemes; Hedge funds; Interconnectedness and concentration; Leverage
summary: Using granular transaction-level data on gilt and derivatives markets, the paper finds that non-bank financial intermediaries (LDI funds, asset managers, hedge funds) are highly exposed to interest rate risk, with derivatives used primarily to amplify rather than hedge exposures. The analysis reveals extreme concentration in interest rate derivatives markets, particularly among hedge funds, which impairs monetary policy transmission and creates financial stability risks.

title: The market for sharing interest rate risk: quantities and asset prices
authors: Umang Khetan; Jian Li; Ioana Neamțu; Ishita Sen
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; LDI funds and pension schemes; Insurers; Dealers and market makers; Asset price volatility
summary: This paper provides the first comprehensive characterisation of end-user demand in the UK interest rate swap market using granular transaction-level data, showing that pension funds and insurers act as natural counterparties to banks and corporations but their demand is highly segmented by maturity. The authors calibrate a preferred-habitat model to quantify how demand imbalances interact with dealer constraints to shape swap spreads, and show that regulatory changes to one sector's hedging mandate generate economically significant spillovers on other sectors' hedging costs.

title: Mispricing in inflation markets
central_concepts: Inflation mispricing; LDI funds and pension schemes; Gilt market; Derivatives markets
summary: Using UK transaction-level data on nominal gilts, inflation-linked bonds, and inflation swaps from 2018-2022, the authors document persistent inflation mispricing of 135 basis points on average and show that liability-driven investor (LDI) pension fund trading activity is a significant driver of this mispricing, while hedge funds respond to mispricing but do not implement full arbitrage strategies due to funding frictions.

title: Macroprudential stress‑test models: a survey
central_concepts: System-wide stress testing; Interconnectedness and concentration; Market-based finance
summary: This survey reviews macroprudential stress-testing models across banking and non-bank financial institutions, identifying key feedback loops and amplification mechanisms. The authors highlight three main modelling challenges: understanding non-bank amplification during stress, developing multi-sectoral models of liquidity dynamics, and incorporating comprehensive financial-real economy interactions.

title: How large are the refinancing risks facing UK corporates from market-based finance?
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Corporate bond markets; Leverage; Financial stability risk
summary: Nearly all UK corporate debt growth since the financial crisis has come from market-based finance rather than bank loans, creating refinancing risks especially for leveraged firms. While near-term refinancing appears manageable, highly leveraged corporates face significant rollover pressures by 2025 and limited ability to adjust balance sheets or access alternative funding if market conditions worsen.

title: Leveraged and inverse ETFs – the exotic side of exchange-traded funds
central_concepts: Open-ended funds; Procyclicality
summary: Leveraged and inverse ETFs generate procyclical rebalancing flows that amplify market moves by forcing sales when markets fall and purchases when they rise, concentrated at market close when liquidity is most vulnerable. While currently posing limited risks to UK financial stability, these products could become destabilizing if they grow significantly in popularity or concentration.

title: Decoding the market for inflation risk
authors: Saleem Bahaj; Robert Czech; Sitong Ding; Ricardo Reis
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Interconnectedness and concentration; Market liquidity; Inflation expectations
summary: The paper decomposes inflation swap prices into liquidity premiums and fundamental inflation expectations using trade-level regulatory data and finds that short-horizon swap prices are dominated by liquidity frictions while long-horizon prices reflect fundamentals. The authors show that pension funds buy inflation protection at long horizons, dealers supply it elastically, and hedge funds drive short-horizon trading, with significant dispersion in dealer beliefs about inflation.

title: Central clearing and the functioning of government bond markets
authors: Yuliya Baranova; Nicholas Vause; Georgia Waddington; Eleanor Holbrook; William Rawstorne; David MacDonald
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Central counterparties; Gilt market; Repo markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: Central clearing of gilt and gilt repo trades could reduce dealer balance sheet exposures by netting offsetting positions, potentially enhancing intermediation capacity during stress. However, recent Basel III reforms have already delivered equivalent netting benefits for cash gilts, and firm-level leverage-ratio constraints suggest clearing alone may not substantially ease dealer capacity constraints during severe episodes like the 2020 dash for cash.

title: An evaluation of the Bank of England’s ILTR operations: comparing the product‑mix auction to alternatives
authors: Grace (in prep., a); Grace (in prep., b); Lings (2013)
central_concepts: Repo markets; Collateral and safe assets; Auction mechanism design
summary: This paper evaluates the Bank of England's Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) auctions using a product-mix auction mechanism, comparing it to simpler alternatives. The analysis of June 2010–January 2014 data finds that the flexible product-mix auction design generated welfare gains of approximately 50% (2 basis points per loan) relative to separate simultaneous auctions and reference price auctions, while larger gains would be expected during periods of market stress.

title: The liquidity state dependence of monetary policy transmission
central_concepts: Monetary policy transmission via markets; Market liquidity; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Term premia
summary: Using transaction-level US Treasury data and high-frequency monetary policy shocks, the paper shows that short-rate increases move long-term yields significantly only when market liquidity is high and arbitrageurs are well-capitalised; this state dependence operates through real term premia rather than inflation expectations. The results imply that arbitrage capital availability is crucial for conventional monetary policy transmission, with implications for the relative effectiveness of tightening versus easing and the use of quantitative easing in distressed markets.

title: Relationship discounts in corporate bond trading
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity
summary: The paper analyzes dealer-client relationships in the OTC corporate bond market using regulatory transaction data, finding that top relationship clients receive transaction-cost discounts of 51% (4.6 basis points) relative to median clients, with discounts more than doubling to above 10 basis points during the COVID-19 dash-for-cash episode. The authors identify two main mechanisms: dealers reward clients who provide liquidity for inventory management, and dealers offer discounts to high-value clients to retain profitable trading volume.

title: Financial stability buy/sell tools: a gilt market case study
central_concepts: Gilt market; LDI funds and pension schemes; Market dysfunction; Fire sales; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: The Bank of England's September–January 2022–23 temporary gilt purchases, totalling £19.3 billion, restored orderly functioning in the dysfunctional gilt market by breaking adverse feedback loops and buying time for leveraged LDI funds to improve their resilience. The intervention was designed around core principles of being temporary, targeted, backstop-priced, and carefully unwound, distinguishing it sharply from monetary policy QE and minimising spillovers to monetary policy stance.

title: How auction design can make a difference: the case of the Bank’s Indexed Long-Term Repo Facility
central_concepts: Repo markets; Central bank backstop facilities; Collateral and safe assets; Auction mechanism design; Welfare maximisation
summary: The paper shows that the Bank of England's Product-Mix Auction (PMA) design for the Indexed Long-Term Repo Facility generates approximately 2 basis points (50%) welfare gains per loan relative to simpler alternative auction designs by automatically adjusting quantities and price spreads across collateral types to market conditions. The PMA's flexibility to respond to stress and participant preferences significantly improves the availability and effectiveness of liquidity insurance compared to fixed-quantity or fixed-price alternatives.

title: Quantitative easing and the functioning of the gilt repo market
authors: Kotidis and van Horen; Joyce et al.; Fatouh et al.; Giansante et al.
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Repo markets; Gilt market; Dealers and market makers
summary: The paper assesses the impact of UK quantitative easing on liquidity provision and pricing in the gilt repo market using difference-in-differences analysis of banks receiving reserve injections. It finds that QE improves repo liquidity, with effects depending on injection size, while the leverage ratio reduces repo intermediation spreads but increases transaction costs.

title: How resilient are UK corporate bond issuers to refinancing risks?
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Corporate bond markets; Refinancing risk
summary: UK corporate bond issuers appear broadly resilient to higher refinancing costs, with around 15% of bonds maturing within two years, but risks are elevated for high-yield borrowers particularly if macroeconomic conditions deteriorate. The analysis finds that refinancing risk depends on maturity profiles, credit ratings, and corporate cash reserves, with some vulnerable firms in the riskiest segments requiring monitoring.

title: An unconventional FX tail risk story
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; FX and FX swap markets; Asset price volatility
summary: The paper examines how central bank unconventional monetary policies (asset purchases, swap lines, forward guidance) impact the tail risk of currency returns across nine advanced economies from 2000-2020, finding a significant cross-border transmission channel through FX markets. Asset purchases and swap lines have particularly large effects on systematic currency tail risk that persist for up to one month and are amplified under joint QE actions.

title: Monetary policy consequences of financial stability interventions: assessing the UK LDI crisis and the central bank policy response
authors: Czech et al.; Pinter; Kodres; Hauser
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Gilt market; Leverage; Fire sales; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: The paper develops the first DSGE model with LDI funds and pension schemes to explain the September 2022 UK gilt crisis, showing how leverage constraints and slow recapitalization of LDIs drive a price-sale spiral in gilts. It quantifies the monetary policy spillovers of the Bank of England's financial stability asset purchases, finding that the temporary, targeted design was crucial to restoring market functioning while avoiding monetary policy impacts, and evaluates alternative tools like NBFI repo lending and macroprudential liquidity buffers.

title: An approach to cleaning MiFID II corporate bond transaction reports
authors: Bank of England staff (author not named)
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Data and transparency on non-banks
summary: This paper develops a systematic approach to cleaning transaction reports on corporate bonds submitted under MiFID II regulations, addressing challenges including non-standardized reporting formats, price and quantity unit variations, and duplicate counterparty reports. The cleaning methodology aims to enhance data quality for robust research on corporate bond market functioning and transaction patterns.

title: Leverage finds a way: a comparison of US Treasury basis trading and the LDI event
authors: Adam Brinley Codd; Daniel Krause; Pierre Ortlieb; Alex Briers
events: March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; US Treasury market; Leverage; Repo markets; Procyclical margin; Fire sales
summary: The paper compares how US and UK financial systems intermediate leveraged asset manager demand: US asset managers use Treasury futures while UK LDI funds use leveraged repo, but both create financial stability risks when collateral calls force deleveraging. The analysis shows that while both intermediation chains perform important functions, leverage requires careful management to prevent fire sales and market dysfunction.

title: LASH risk and interest rates
central_concepts: Liquidity mismatch; LDI funds and pension schemes; Insurers; Derivatives markets; Repo markets; Margin and collateral calls; Leverage
summary: This paper introduces LASH (Liquidity After Solvency Hedging) risk, a form of liquidity risk arising when institutions hedge solvency risk through derivatives, creating liquidity needs precisely when solvency improves. Using UK regulatory data on repo and swap transactions from 2019-2022, the authors show that low interest rates increase LASH risk among pension funds and insurers, and that pre-crisis LASH risk predicts substantial gilt sales during the September 2022 UK bond market crisis, amplifying the yield spike.

title: ‘No one length fits all’ – haircuts in the repo market
authors: Carlos Cañon Salazar; Joshua Lillis; Miruna-Daniela Ivan; Eduardo Maqui
events: March 2023 banking stress; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Repo markets; Collateral and safe assets; Procyclical margin; Gilt market
summary: Using novel SFTR transaction-level data, the authors show that repo haircuts in the gilt market are primarily driven by counterparty credit risk but also reflect collateral characteristics such as maturity and market risk. They find evidence of procyclical haircut increases during the 2022 LDI crisis and note that low haircuts on hedge fund transactions may indicate substantial leveraging without appropriate risk mitigation.

title: Futures under stress: how did gilt futures behave in the LDI crisis?
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; September 2022 LDI episode; Market liquidity; Gilt market; Market dysfunction
summary: During the September 2022 LDI crisis, gilt futures liquidity deteriorated sharply following the fiscal statement on 23 September, with orderbook depth falling and price impact rising, though the Bank of England's 28 September gilt purchase announcement brought gradual improvement over five months. The paper uses high-frequency electronic orderbook data to show that while yield repricing occurred continuously without trading gaps, market makers substantially reduced their intermediation capacity during the stress.

title: Collateral demand in wholesale funding markets
events: March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Repo markets; Collateral and safe assets; Liquidity mismatch
summary: The paper builds and structurally estimates a model of repo trading using detailed transaction data from the Sterling gilt repo market to study how collateral demand interacts with funding demand. It finds that collateral demand impedes repo market functioning because firms needing funding tend to be the same firms that value collateral highly, reducing trading volumes and gains to trade, particularly in financial stress.

title: Measuring capital at risk with financial contagion: two-sector model with banks and insurers
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Insurers; Fire sales; Interconnectedness and concentration; System-wide stress testing
summary: The paper develops a microstructural stress-testing methodology for the UK financial system combining banks and insurers to quantify capital at risk from correlated corporate default shocks, incorporating financial contagion through fire-sales and solvency channels. The authors find that since Covid-19, the UK financial system has improved in profit expectations and tail losses, with insurers more affected by credit and traded risk losses while banks suffer more from fire-sale losses.

title: Fire sales of safe assets
central_concepts: Fire sales; LDI funds and pension schemes; Gilt market; Liquidity mismatch; Balance-sheet segmentation
summary: This paper uses comprehensive regulatory data on UK gilt, repo, and derivatives transactions to identify the mechanisms of the September-October 2022 gilt market fire sale. The authors find that LDI forced selling caused price discounts of up to 10%, accounting for approximately half the decline in long-dated gilt prices, and that balance-sheet segmentation between LDI funds and their pension investors—combined with coordination frictions in pooled LDIs—prevented rapid recapitalization and amplified forced sales.

title: Whose asset sales matter?
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Hedge funds; Fire sales; Asset price volatility; Information asymmetry
summary: Using novel UK bond trading data, the authors develop a measure of exogenous selling pressure and show that the price impact of asset sales depends critically on who is selling: dealers and hedge funds generate significantly larger price impacts than other investors of the same size. They rationalize this finding using a model of differentially informed investors, where counterparties demand larger price discounts when trading with perceived informed traders.

title: What caused the LDI crisis?
authors: Danny Walker; Gabor Pinter; Emil Siriwardane
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Gilt market; Leverage; Fire sales; Balance-sheet segmentation
summary: In September 2022, UK gilt prices fell sharply following a fiscal expansion announcement, with LDI funds accounting for approximately half the decline through forced gilt sales. The authors find that balance sheet segmentation and operational frictions between pension schemes and LDI funds, rather than excessive leverage per se, prevented timely capital injections and forced liquidations, particularly among pooled LDI funds.

title: Why do UK companies raise market-based finance debt?
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Corporate bond markets; Private credit and private equity
summary: Since 2007–08, nearly all net increase in UK corporate debt has come from market-based finance; this analysis of 10,000 MBF issuance deals finds that bonds and syndicated loans dominate, with companies raising bonds for operations and refinancing, private credit for acquisitions, and syndicated loans for varied purposes. The paper identifies refinancing risk in the £425 billion stock, noting that if companies cannot refinance debt raised for operational purposes at market prices, they may reduce investment or employment with real economic consequences.

title: Caring for the ‘future’
events: August 2024 volatility spike; March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Market liquidity
summary: SONIA futures are critical to sterling interest rate markets and monetary policy transmission, but experienced severe liquidity deterioration in 2022 that has only partially recovered. Market depth remains materially lower than pre-hiking cycle levels despite improvements in open interest and volumes, with UK-specific factors—particularly the timing of data releases outside market hours—potentially constraining further recovery and market-maker participation.

title: SONIA: steady as she goes
authors: Joanna McLafferty; Kirstine McMillan; Joseph Smart
central_concepts: Money markets
summary: The SONIA reference rate remained flat at 5.2000% for over three months from May 2024, an unprecedented occurrence explained by the trimmed-mean calculation methodology concentrating the central 50% of volume at a single rate. The authors argue this flatlining reflects normal market mechanics and reserve-draining dynamics rather than dysfunction, as the market continues to function with adequate depth and diverse participation.

title: A simple model of the effects of entity and activity constraints on alternative investment funds
authors: Leo Fernandes; Harkeerit Kalsi; Nicholas Vause; Matthew Downer; Sarah Ek; Sebastian Maxted
central_concepts: Hedge funds; Leverage; Margin and collateral calls; Financial stability risk
summary: The authors use a portfolio choice model to compare entity-level leverage limits and activity-level margin requirements as tools for reducing financial stability risks from alternative investment funds. Entity-level leverage limits can inadvertently shift funds towards riskier investments and concentrated strategies, whereas activity-level constraints with risk-sensitive margin requirements can more effectively reduce risk without inducing harmful portfolio reallocation.

title: Firm risk premia and monetary policy transmission
central_concepts: Financial stability risk; Procyclicality; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The paper shows that firms' excess bond premia (EBPs), which measure the risk-premium component of credit spreads, shape how monetary policy transmission affects firm investment. Lower-EBP firms increase investment more in response to monetary easing despite experiencing smaller credit-spread compressions, while the distribution of EBPs across firms determines aggregate monetary policy effectiveness.

title: Financial stability at the Bank of England
events: March 2023 banking stress; March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Financial stability risk; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: The Bank of England protects financial stability through macroprudential policy, microprudential regulation, resolution authority powers, and balance sheet operations, coordinated across the Financial Policy Committee, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Financial Market Infrastructure Directorate. Recent episodes including the 2020 dash for cash, 2022 LDI crisis, and 2023 banking stress demonstrate the importance of system-wide resilience and coordination between financial stability and monetary policy committees.

title: The contribution of the Financial Policy Committee to UK financial stability
authors: Bank of England Financial Policy Committee
events: Brexit; March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Financial stability risk; Macroprudential policy for non-banks
summary: The article describes the Financial Policy Committee's role as the UK's macroprudential authority, established to identify and mitigate systemic risks to financial stability. The FPC has evolved over its first decade to address vulnerabilities in both banking and market-based finance sectors through various policy tools including capital requirements, recommendations, and stress testing.

title: Shining a light on private equity backed corporates in four findings
authors: Neha Bora; Sarah Burkinshaw; Alice Crundwell; Tuli Saha
central_concepts: Private credit and private equity; Leverage; Refinancing risk; Default risk and risk premium
summary: Using a novel dataset of 9,000 UK private equity–backed corporates, the authors find that PE-backed firms account for around 15% of UK corporate debt and employ over two million people, but exhibit higher vulnerability to default than other corporates and rely heavily on shorter-tenor private credit and leveraged loans, creating refinancing risks in a higher-rate environment.

title: Sharing interest rate risk: who is trading and what affects the costs?
authors: Ioana Neamțu; Umang Khetan; Jian Li; Ishita Sen
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Interest rate exposure; LDI funds and pension schemes; Dealers and market makers; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: Using confidential Bank of England trade-level data, the authors analyse the interest rate swap market to identify how different sectors hedge interest rate risk and how demand imbalances between natural counterparties affect swap pricing. They find that pension funds and insurers receive fixed rates while banks and corporations pay fixed rates, and that dealer imbalances and sector-specific demand shocks significantly influence swap spreads.

title: Nonbank lenders as global shock absorbers
authors: David Elliott; Ralf Meisenzahl; José-Luis Peydró
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Corporate bond markets; Monetary policy transmission via markets; Bank–non-bank linkages
summary: Nonbank lenders increase international dollar lending to non-US corporates when US monetary policy tightens, offsetting some of the contractionary spillovers from Fed policy that banks would otherwise amplify. This substitution from bank to nonbank credit helps stabilize corporate investment and employment, but may involve a trade-off with financial stability if nonbanks are more fragile during crises.

title: The yield curve impact of government debt issuance surprises and the implications for QT
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Gilt market; Portfolio balance effects; Duration risk; Local supply channel; Government debt issuance; Yield curve
summary: The paper analyses UK government debt auction announcements to quantify the impact of Bank of England quantitative tightening (QT) on the yield curve, finding that yield reactions operate through both duration risk and local supply channels and vary significantly with market stress. Under low market stress, a fully unanticipated QT programme mimicking the Bank's 2022 plan would raise 10-year yields by 20 basis points, with passive unwinding having broadly equivalent effects to active sales.

title: Zero-day options and financial market vulnerability
central_concepts: Derivatives markets; Equity markets; Dealers and market makers
summary: Zero-day options—contracts expiring within a single trading day—have grown to represent approximately half of S&P 500 options volume, driven by retail participation and market design changes. The rapid expansion raises concerns about potential systemic risks including hedging-induced volatility, margin call deficiencies, and capital requirement gaps, though recent evidence suggests these risks may be limited and require further data collection.

title: How has the changing cash-collateral backdrop affected repo markets?
central_concepts: Repo markets; Gilt market; Collateral and safe assets
summary: The paper examines how declining cash reserves and increased gilt issuance have shifted sterling repo markets from collateral scarcity to collateral plenty, resulting in elevated general collateral repo rates and upward period-end spikes as dealers seek to place collateral and borrow cash. The repo market has continued to function well despite these shifts, with the Bank's Short-Term Repo facility providing a backstop for interest rate control.

title: Stable gilts and stable prices: assessing the Bank of England’s response to the LDI crisis
central_concepts: LDI funds and pension schemes; Fire sales; Gilt market; Market dysfunction; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The authors develop a DSGE model with LDI funds to assess the Bank of England's 2022 gilt market intervention, finding that temporary asset purchases worth 0.9% of GDP stabilised the market without materially affecting monetary policy despite inflation above 10%. They show the fire-sale mechanism was driven by LDI deleveraging constraints and illiquid gilt markets, and that the temporary nature of purchases was crucial to avoiding persistent monetary policy spillovers.

title: Topography of the FX derivatives market: a view from London
central_concepts: FX and FX swap markets; Hedge funds; Net FX derivatives exposures; Basis trades
summary: This paper provides the first detailed firm-level analysis of FX derivatives market behaviour in the UK, the world's largest FX trading centre, using transaction-level data from 2015-2020. It finds that pension funds, insurers, and non-financial corporations primarily use FX derivatives for hedging, while hedge funds predominantly speculate using carry trades and momentum strategies.

title: QT versus QE: who is in when the central bank is out?
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; LDI funds and pension schemes; Insurers; Gilt market; Monetary policy transmission via markets; Preferred habitat demand
summary: The paper analyses how preferred habitat demand from pension funds and insurance companies affects the transmission of QE and QT through central bank auctions and secondary gilt markets. It finds that PH demand dampens dealer bidding and lowers yields during QE, but plays a negligible role during QT, an asymmetry explained by increased government bond issuance since Covid-19.

title: Dealers, information, and liquidity crises in safe assets
events: March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Dealers and market makers; Gilt market; LDI funds and pension schemes; Market dysfunction; Margin and collateral calls; Market liquidity; Information asymmetry
summary: During the 2022 UK LDI crisis, dealers substantially reduced trade costs for informed clients while raising costs and restricting liquidity for uninformed investors, contrary to traditional adverse selection models. This information-chasing behavior by dealers reallocated scarce liquidity away from the broader market, deepening market-wide liquidity shortages and amplifying the crisis.

title: What has driven increased leveraged loan activity over 2024?
authors: Owen Clark; Edward Egan; Sarah Munson; George Pugh
central_concepts: Private credit and private equity; Market dysfunction
summary: Institutional leveraged loan activity tripled in 2024, primarily driven by repricing and refinancing rather than new M&A/LBO issuance, as strong investor demand benefited from resilient US growth and fewer expected rate cuts. Spreads compressed significantly despite elevated default rates, raising financial stability risks from reduced risk premia and liquidity mismatches in leveraged loan funds, though near-term refinancing needs have improved moderately.

title: Why do government bond yields drift when news is on its way?
authors: Danny Walker; Dong Lou; Gabor Pinter; Semih Üslü
central_concepts: Gilt market; Dealers and market makers; Hedge funds
summary: Government bond yields drift upward in the two days before anticipated monetary policy announcements and macroeconomic data releases in the UK, driven by dealers' reluctance to hold inventory and hedge funds' pullback from buying bonds ahead of news. This pre-news drift, which has cumulatively raised yields by 2 percentage points since 1997, is concentrated when bond issuance precedes news and may distort the signal policymakers draw from market rates.

title: Monitoring collateral calls
events: August 2024 volatility spike; March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Margin and collateral calls; Market-based finance; Repo markets; Derivatives markets; LDI funds and pension schemes
summary: The Bank of England monitored collateral calls on non-bank financial institutions during January 2025 gilt market stress, estimating £7 billion in total calls (£4 billion on repo, £3 billion on swaps), substantially smaller than during previous crises. The analysis found no signs of forced asset sales, contrasting sharply with March 2020 and September 2022 episodes where collateral spirals amplified market dysfunction.

title: Investors as a liquidity backstop in corporate bond markets
authors: Not explicitly listed in provided text
events: March 2023 banking stress; March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Dealer balance-sheet constraints; Market liquidity; Hedge funds
summary: Investors provide liquidity to dealers in corporate bond markets by acting as counterparties when dealers seek to unwind positions, reducing dealers' balance sheet costs and stabilizing trading. During the March 2020 Dash-for-Cash, bonds where investors stopped providing this liquidity saw transaction costs rise by 38%, and the composition of liquidity providers—particularly the presence of flexible-mandate hedge funds versus constrained insurers—significantly shapes trading resilience.

title: Collateral re-use: unveiling the risk of delivery failures and higher volatility in the repo market
events: March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Repo markets; Gilt market; Market dysfunction; Asset price volatility
summary: The paper examines collateral re-use in the gilt repo market, finding that while it reduces funding costs in normal conditions, elevated re-use increases the risk of delivery failures and amplifies repo rate volatility during stress periods. Analysis of UK money market data from January 2017 to April 2023 shows collateral re-use averaged 3.5% and spiked during March 2020 and September 2022 episodes, with a positive correlation (~53%) between re-use and repo rate volatility.

title: How is the transition to a repo-led framework progressing?
central_concepts: Repo markets; Money markets; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: The Bank of England is transitioning to a repo-led monetary operating framework as sterling reserves decline through quantitative tightening and TFSME repayments. Usage of the Short-Term Repo (STR) and Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) facilities has increased substantially, with the STR helping to keep overnight money market rates close to Bank Rate despite structural shifts in the cash-collateral balance from increased gilt issuance.

title: Shining a light on hidden leverage: using transaction level data to monitor leveraged positions in the non-bank financial system
central_concepts: Leverage; Derivatives markets; Interconnectedness and concentration; Data and transparency on non-banks
summary: The document examines how transaction-level EMIR Trade Repository data can be used to monitor hidden leverage in non-bank financial institutions, using the Archegos case as a motivating example. It describes monitoring tools that track large and rapidly growing derivative exposures across counterparties to identify concentrations of risk and early warning signals of systemic vulnerability.

title: The real economy effects of QE through the corporate bond market
authors: Joyce, Tong, Woods (2011); Todorov (2020); Fatouh, Markose, Giansante (2021)
central_concepts: Central bank backstop facilities; Corporate bond markets; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The Bank of England's QE operations reduced corporate bond yields and increased investment-grade bond issuance between 2009 and 2021, but companies used the additional funds for share buybacks and debt restructuring rather than real investment. Direct corporate bond purchases under the CBPS lowered eligible bond yields by 40-60 basis points but did not translate into lower borrowing costs or higher issuance in the primary market.

title: Straight and narrow: recent changes in SONIA and why we care
authors: Victoria Saporta; Joanna McLafferty; Ashley Young; Kirstine McMillan; Callum Ashworth; Abhilash Barman
central_concepts: Money markets; Repo markets; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: SONIA, the Sterling Overnight Index Average, is a key benchmark for sterling unsecured overnight rates and a crucial conduit for monetary policy transmission to the wider economy. The paper analyses recent movements in the SONIA-Bank Rate spread as sterling reserves have declined through quantitative tightening, finding that the spread has narrowed in line with historical relationships, with the Bank's repo facilities acting as a backstop to prevent excessive money market disruption.

title: Gilt market liquidity in April 2025
events: March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Gilt market; Market liquidity
summary: The Bank of England monitored gilt market liquidity during April 2025 volatility and found a temporary, modest deterioration that remained within historical ranges and was commensurate with the level of volatility—significantly less severe than the 2020 dash for cash or 2022 LDI episodes. The analysis demonstrates how quantitative metrics (bid-offer spreads, Amihud, yield curve noise, order book depth) combined with qualitative market intelligence provide a holistic framework for monitoring core market functioning.

title: Repo dealer-driven bond mispricing
central_concepts: Repo markets; Gilt market; Dealers and market makers; Market liquidity; Market dysfunction; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: Using proprietary UK repo and gilt market data from 2016-2022, the paper demonstrates that dealer market power and persistent shocks to influential dealers account for significant bond mispricing (0.5-4 percentage points) and affect market-wide liquidity. The findings highlight how microstructure frictions in bilateral OTC repo markets spill over to gilt pricing and suggest the need for enhanced monitoring and transparency in these core funding markets.

title: Trading relationships in FX derivatives: lessons from Credit Suisse’s collapse
central_concepts: FX and FX swap markets; Dealers and market makers; OTC market structure; Dealer-client relationships; Trading relationships and persistence
summary: Using granular transaction-level data from the UK EMIR trade repository, this paper documents that dealer-client trading relationships in the OTC FX derivatives market are persistent, and that clients relying more heavily on a dealer pay higher spreads, suggesting dealers charge markups to clients that search less intensely. When Credit Suisse collapsed in March 2023, clients who had relied more heavily on Credit Suisse were able to substitute to other existing dealer relationships without incurring additional costs, indicating that relationship persistence did not prevent reallocating activity when a relationship dealer came under stress.

title: Monetary policy, state-dependent bank capital requirements and the role of non-bank financial intermediaries
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Margin policy reforms; Asset price volatility; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The paper develops a DSGE model showing that non-bank financial institutions amplify the contractionary effects of monetary policy through the asset price channel, with strongest effects in economic downturns and under zero lower bound conditions. Despite short-run vulnerabilities, a greater share of NBFI lending is associated with higher long-run welfare due to lower regulatory burdens.

title: Learning to navigate bumps in the road
central_concepts: Repo markets; Money markets; Central bank backstop facilities
summary: The Bank of England's transition to a repo-led, demand-driven framework for reserve supply is progressing as intended, with rising usage of its market-wide facilities (ILTR and STR) and stable short-term money market rates anchored to Bank Rate. Market participants are adapting to lower reserve levels and higher gilt supply, though temporary volatility spikes—such as in October 2025—reveal ongoing learning about liquidity forecasting and the framework's operation.

title: Who owns the buildings where Britain shops, works – and stores its data?
central_concepts: Commercial real estate; Market-based finance; Private credit and private equity
summary: The authors develop a new measure of UK commercial real estate ownership by investor type from 2016 to 2025 Q3, showing a market increasingly dominated by overseas and private equity investors, with shifting sectoral composition toward logistics, residential, and data centres. They argue that ownership structure matters for financial stability because leveraged or short-horizon owners can amplify downturns through refinancing pressures, fire sales, and collateral channels.

title: Retail investors’ participation in the gilt market
central_concepts: Gilt market; Market-based finance
summary: Retail investor holdings of gilts have grown significantly in recent years, concentrated in ultra-short-maturity, low-coupon bonds where they can comprise a meaningful share of individual bond free float. While retail positions remain modest in aggregate (under 4% of gilts in issue) and have limited impact on overall market liquidity, they create yield curve distortions and concentrated holdings in specific bonds that warrant continued monitoring for financial stability and monetary policy transmission.

title: Monetary policy, state-dependent bank capital requirements and the role of non-bank financial intermediaries
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Dealers and market makers; Monetary policy transmission via markets; Financial stability risk
summary: Using a DSGE model with state-dependent bank capital requirements, the authors find that while non-bank financial institutions enhance long-term welfare by improving credit allocation and market efficiency, they amplify the contractionary effects of monetary policy and significantly worsen GDP outcomes during severe downturns. The balance-sheet channel dominates over the competitive lending channel, meaning NBFIs cannot fully offset reduced bank credit when bond prices fall, particularly in the worst 5% of economic scenarios.

title: Bond financing conditions and economic activity in the UK: aggregate and firm-level evidence
authors: Eduardo Maqui; Nicholas Vause; Márcia Silva-Pereira
central_concepts: Corporate bond markets; Credit to the real economy; Market liquidity; Leverage; Procyclicality; Monetary policy transmission via markets
summary: The paper shows that corporate bond financing conditions, measured by the Excess Bond Premium (EBP), significantly affect UK macroeconomic outcomes and firm investment, with particularly large impacts on highly leveraged firms reliant on bond finance. The effect operates through a market-based finance propagation channel where shocks to bond financing conditions trigger sharp cuts in investment by bond-dependent firms, amplifying the sensitivity of aggregate investment.

title: Resilience and readiness across the Sterling Monetary Framework
central_concepts: Repo markets; Central bank backstop facilities; Collateral and safe assets; Liquidity preparedness
summary: The Bank of England describes the normalisation of its Sterling Monetary Framework as facilities usage broadens and reserves decline through quantitative tightening, with firms demonstrating operational readiness to access liquidity through repo. The Bank recalibrates bilateral facilities and introduces modern infrastructure to ensure firms can confidently monetise collateral across market-wide and on-demand operations in a demand-driven system.

title: A simulation framework for sterling money market funds: estimating redemption capacity and evaluating liquidity requirements
central_concepts: Money market funds; Liquidity mismatch; Run risk; Money market fund reform; Threshold effects
summary: This paper develops a simulation framework for sterling money market funds (MMFs) to estimate their redemption capacity and failure probability under various redemption shocks and market-liquidity scenarios. The author finds that resilience depends critically on the timing of outflows and market depth, that removing threshold effects near the 30% regulatory minimum substantially improves resilience, and that optimal buffers concentrate around 40% weekly liquid assets with diminishing returns beyond.

title: Quantitative tightening? Britain’s 1980s experiment with overfunding
central_concepts: Monetary policy transmission via markets; Overfunding; Gilt market; Portfolio balance channel
summary: This paper examines the Bank of England's overfunding policy in the early 1980s—issuance of government bonds in excess of fiscal needs as an active monetary policy tool—as a historical analogue to modern quantitative tightening. The analysis finds that overfunding raised long-term gilt yields through portfolio balance effects but reduced short-term rates through signalling effects, with these offsetting forces producing limited impacts on inflation and monetary aggregates.

title: From Mayfair to the Caymans: mapping and quantifying non-bank default risk in UK markets
events: March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Hedge funds; Market-based finance; Leverage; Interconnectedness and concentration
summary: The paper maps non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) active in UK markets from 2016–2025 using Legal Entity Identifier codes and probability-of-default (PD) estimates, finding that default risk is heavily concentrated in hedge funds, particularly those offshore in the Cayman Islands, with elevated and widening PDs that exceed stress episode levels. The authors argue that high and volatile default risk in leveraged offshore hedge funds, combined with their exposures to key global markets and interconnectedness with UK dealers, presents vulnerabilities requiring enhanced surveillance, counterparty risk management, and international coordination.

title: SoS! The overnight bilateral liquidity provision of non-bank financial institutions to banks
authors: Elio Cucullo; Andrew Clare; Angela Gallo
central_concepts: Market-based finance; Repo markets; Bank–non-bank linkages; Leverage
summary: Using transaction-level data from the UK gilt repo market, the authors show that non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) supply 6-12 times more overnight liquidity to banks than interbank lenders do, with the cost of NBFI funding shifting from cheaper to more expensive and volatile after 2022. They identify two mechanisms: an opportunity-cost channel where higher short-term rates lead NBFIs to pass increased costs to banks, and a balance-sheet constraint channel where higher long-term rates tighten NBFIs' leverage constraints, amplifying pricing volatility and reducing liquidity elasticity.

title: Gilt edged resilience: strengthening liquidity provision in the repo market
events: March 2020 dash for cash; September 2022 LDI episode
central_concepts: Gilt market; Repo markets; Hedge funds; Margin and collateral calls
summary: The document argues that the gilt repo market requires enhanced resilience through greater central clearing and minimum haircuts on non-centrally cleared transactions to prevent future stress episodes like March 2020 and September 2022. It addresses three key industry challenges to proposed reforms, emphasizing that netting benefits from clearing are significant, near-zero haircuts reflect competitive pressures rather than prudent risk management, and procyclical margin in centrally cleared markets can be mitigated through careful design and preparedness.

title: One dollar, many prices: dealer-specific pricing of synthetic dollar funding
central_concepts: FX and FX swap markets; Dealers and market makers; Dealer balance-sheet constraints
summary: Using transaction-level FX forward data, the paper shows that dealers charge substantially different prices for synthetic dollar funding depending on which dealer intermediates the trade, with sell-side dealers pricing 2.5 basis points higher than buy-side dealers on average and up to 11.8 basis points at short maturities. After controlling for client-dealer relationships and transaction characteristics, differences in dollar funding conditions across major dealers explain little of this price dispersion, suggesting that dealer market power and intermediation rather than funding scarcity drive the observed pricing heterogeneity.

title: Finance, growth and productive investment: what is the FPC assessing in 2026?
authors: Bank of England Financial Policy Committee
central_concepts: Credit to the real economy; Private credit and private equity; Financial stability risk
summary: The FPC examines how the UK financial system supports productive investment and high-growth firms, finding that financing challenges reflect not a shortage of capital but mismatches between the types of finance available and firms' needs. A more diverse financial ecosystem including capital markets and non-bank lenders can better match firms to suitable financing, though growing bank–non-bank linkages create new channels for systemic risk transmission.

title: When the financial system becomes searchable
central_concepts: Leverage; Margin and collateral calls; Liquidity mismatch; Fire sales; Interconnectedness and concentration; Collateral and safe assets; AI-driven surveillance and optimisation
summary: The paper explores how advances in artificial intelligence could make the financial system more 'searchable', allowing both private agents and authorities to identify previously invisible connections between vulnerabilities like leverage, illiquid markets, and collateral constraints. It outlines scenarios where AI agents could discover routes through the system that exploit fragmented information or create hidden exposures across legal entities and jurisdictions, and argues that financial authorities must develop AI-assisted stress testing and observability requirements to match these new capabilities.
